review_title: Touchscreen Freezes After a Few Swipes
review_text:
Brand new unit, these things have been getting made for years, not sure why they haven't figured out this bug yet. Considering how long this product has been out, I'm not expecting this bug to be fixed in the next couple of weeks when it's such a mature product at this point.

Note: The first thing I did when I got this device was download the iphone app, pair this watch to my phone, and do an update on the watch to the latest software.

The main issue, after starting a bike ride, outdoor run, or anything else, for the first time the watch connects to your phone and updates "A-GPS" whatever that means. It's a 1-3 minute process and then it's ready to go. Immediately after this update I'm unable to do more than 5-20 swipe gestures to navigate through the interface before the touchscreen becomes completely unresponsive.

No amount of swipes or taps will recover it from this state. The side button works, and allows you to get all the way to the home menu, but the screen will still be unresponsive. After a few minutes pass the devices goes to sleep, you need to press the side button to wake it and the screen is magically working again... within 10-20 seconds it's frozen again.

This made trying to use this at the gym increddibly frustrating, starting a workout, checking stats, doing anything, usually resulted in the unit freezing, and even self-rebooting a couple times. All on day one.

As I got ready to pack this thing back up to ship it back to wherever it came from I performed a factory reset on the unit. It worked great! I could swipe, tap, and gesture till my heart's content. It seemed that the problem had vanished, I could swipe for minutes and not have a single screen freeze incident.

Then I started a "run" workout. My watch showed the screen "Updating A-GPS", after a minute or 2 the workout started. I canceled the workout. As I started navigating through the menu it became immediately clear that the issue was back, screen freezing so bad I could hardly navigate to the menu to do another factory reset to finally get rid of this time and money wasting device.

The promotional materials are very exciting and compelling for this device, especially at this price point. But I do not have the patience to endure this horrible product's software to try some of the more exciting features.

On the plus, I could see my frustration with this product literally raising my heart-rate.

One final note, while I was cranking away on an elliptical at my gym my heart rate according to the elliptical was 185 (yeah, high I know, but I was huffing and puffing and dripping sweat) while the watch said it was 112.. I've seen other reviews that seem to indicate the inaccuracy of this reading.

review_text:
First off, I am very saddened to see my beloved Bip fail on me. It has lived up beyond expectations with its long battery life, easy to read screen under the harshest sunlight, and decent fitness tracking.

So, why the downside?

Just yesterday, I felt an odd sensation on my wrist yesterday. It felt as if the strap had failed - as I felt the shifting of weight on my wrist. Lo and behold! When I looked down to my wrist, I found that the screen of the watch had separated like a lid on a jack in the box!

The watch has never been abused, as the screen and the body is devoid of any scratches or dings. Taking a closer look at how the watch face could have separated, reveals that it is held in place with what appears to be an extremely thin piece of double-sided tape. I live in Southern California - where the average temperature hovers between the 60s and 70s year round. To be fair, there are days when temperatures hit double digits for a few days. However, I certainly do not live anywhere near a place that can be considered to have extreme temperatures.

My thinking is that normal temperature variations over time have caused the watch face to come off of the Bip. Having owned watches ranging from Swiss crafted Omega to cheap dollar store variety digital watches, I can't think of a single one failing in this manner.

I am within the warranty period. But, if this is the standard of manufacturing, I am leery of a replacement or repaired unit lasting much longer than a few months.

I've submitted a request for warranty support. Their response will tell whether I got an odd lemon, or the old adage, "You get what you pay for" holds true.

--- Followup on customer non-service Aril 10, 2019 --

Went to the company US website to process an RMA for a warranty return. It should be pretty easy, right? Guess again. I opened a ticket for the incident, which was on a Wednesday. I added screenshots of the defective product, a copy of my Amazon invoice.

Late Sunday evening, an agent replied, requesting that I complete an Excel spreadsheet that he/she attached. The fields that I am to complete is asking for what I already submitted, minus the serial number, which I did not initially include. But, the web form for the ticket did not request this information.

The agent replied on my late Sunday evening, which would likely mean that he/she is answering on their Monday morning in China. Why assume China? For one thing, the font used in the Excel sheet is a Chinese font.

So, I grudgingly complete the spreadsheet details and reply back on my Monday. Since then, the agent has been MIA.

I realize that even the best products can suffer defects. However, this complete lack of customer service leads me to believe that this company is neither ready or fit to do business in the US with the big boys.

Lowering my score to a single star from two. And, if you want a product that won't be tossed in the trash in a few months, look for a product sold and supported by someone competent.

—- Final update April 16, 2019

Buyer beware. My frustration with Huami/Amazfit USA drove me to my final option. I reached out to Amazon customer support. I provided an Amazon agent with copies of my communication regarding my warranty request.

Amazon took care of me. Consider me a vocal activist on why you should NOT buy anything from Huami/Amazfit USA. I for one will refuse to buy anything made by them, nor recommend that anyone else make the mistake of buying this.

Needless to say, there is a complete lack of communication from this manufacturer. They get a resounding F for customer service.

review_title: Not ready for the US market.... And then the blue tooth failed
review_text:
Pros:
The watch is easy, cheap, and with excellent battery life.
It's easy because the watch is really limited with apps and other "cool" features that we expect on a smart watch these days. It has exactly what I need though. Notification for texts, phone calls, emails etc, but without the ability reply through the watch. Suited me fine, since I never did that on my LG sport watch either. It has the basic features that I want for fitness tracking, which is 90% of my use. Onboard GPS, pedometer, distance tracking, HR, sleep tracking, calorie burn etc.

Battery life that lasts weeks and that's with an always-on screen. Simply amazing and I cannot emphasize enough how important battery life meant for me. I stopped using my LG sport (and others before that), because I got tired of always had to charge it, forget it at home because it was charging, or run out of juice when I forgot to charge it.
Not a problem with this watch. I just charge it once a month and it just dissolves into the background.

It's very light weight. I didn't realize how this made a difference to me before, but I do enjoy that I hardly notice that I'm wearing it. I wanted to track my sleep, but my LG sport was just too heavy and uncomfortable to wear at night. This one is perfect for me. Granted that's because it's made of plastic. It does make it look somewhat cheap, but I think the black version looks fine. Nothing flashy, but that's just perfect in my opinion.
After a month of wearing it I don't have any scratches or other issue with the screen or case.

Cons:
So I do really like this watch for all the above reasons, but in my opinion they really failed on some of the key features for a watch with "fit" in their name.
I can't comment on the accuracy of GPS, HR, pedometer or distance tracking, but others have said it seems pretty good. However my biggest disappointment is the calorie burn is so catastrophically wrong. I went for a 4.5 mile walk (18min/mile) and it says that I only burned 302 calories. I measured the same walk with Strava and got 620 calories burned. Online calc says about 560 calories, for my weight, height, gender etc. Seems also BMR is not added to any calorie burn. I expect from any fitness tracker to be able to calculate BMR + activity for a total calorie burn for the day. When I read on my watch that I've only burned 600 cal at the end of the day, then I just can't take this watch seriously. I hope they can fix this in future updates, hopefully the very next update.

I've only used the walking and running activity mode features on the watch and it seems to work fine in my opinion, but I kinda bummed there's no pace counter on the screen. I would want to see my minutes/mile pace with just a quick glance on the watch.

The available watch screen faces are very limited, but I feel there's a number of them that look just fine to me. However there's almost nothing out there that cater to the US market. Having the date month/day, 12hr, distance in miles.
There's a couple of apps out there that allows you to design your own and I actually tried to do this by copying one that I liked and just flipped month/day. You can also use the same app to switch between 12hr/24hr, but I personally prefer 24hr.
Where it lacks and why I say it's not ready for the US market is the distance counting. The Mifit app can switch between metric and imperial settings and that works somewhat. When in activity mode, I can see my run etc in miles. It does show temperature in Fahrenheit on the primary screen if I use that on there, but for whatever reason it will only show my distance in Km on the primary screen no-matter what even though I have set the Mifit setting for imperial (US) units. If anyone knows how to fix this, I'll be glad to know.

My primary watch face has steps, distance (in Km), date, time, calorie burn, HR, and week day. I just ignore the distance and just measure my activity by steps/day. The calorie burn hurts that it's so wrong, but I kept it there as well as distance in the hopes that it will be fixed in a future update..... but then the blue tooth failed. The watch won't connect for any reason now. Tried factory reset etc, but nothing works and I can only assume that the blue tooth just stopped working on the watch. It's a cheap watch, but it should at least last a year or two right? Luckily it failed on me within 30 days, and I'm able to return it to amazon as a defect.
I really want to like this watch. I might try get another one and hope it's better quality as well getting the update that will fix the calorie count and other features.

I want to be notified when I get a text or a call, I want steps tracked, and I want my heart rate monitored. Not having to recharge the watch every 2 days would be great, too. On paper, the Bip meets all my criteria perfectly. In practice, however, it's a much different story.

Now, the watch looks nice, and the faces are simple but classy. The problem comes when you get into functionality. The weather app would not sync, no matter what I did. Then, all of a sudden, 2 days after I bought it, it finally did sync. Beats me as to why it took 2 days, but better late than never, right?

The thing that finally made me return the watch was the way the screen froze up. I wouldn't be swiping through the menus on the watch face but for about 30 seconds when the face would stop responding to touch. The watch itself didn't freeze, as pressing the crown would return the watch to the main screen, but the watch would not register any touch input. It kept doing this, and I'd have to let it go back to sleep and then wait for like a minute before I could wake it up and it would start registering touch input again.

I know this is an $80 watch, and I shouldn't expect much, and I didn't. But I do expect the watch to do basic functions as advertised, like work when I swipe around on it. Honestly, I'm sticking with my Ticwatch E. It's $30 more and it actually works, minus the insane battery life of the Bip. review_title: Both HR AND BP are completely UNRELIABLE
review_text:
I cant even with this watch- its cheap and may have *some* redeeming features such as weather, messages, time…

But NO WAY IS THIS EVEN CLOSE TO BEING ACCURATE ON BP OR HR. I doubt that steps are anywhere near accurate either.

My home BP monitor is consistent and is known for being higher on both sys/dia by 10/5 points (calibrated in the doctor’s office AND with my own knowledge of taking BP with cuff/stetho - as a former EMT).

This watch is measuring way off - over 15/10!

Then when I switch the watch to the inside of my wrist- it drops both down (still elevated though) closer to the home monitor I have.

HR is also off by a wild 10-20 pts.

So if anyone is looking for any BP/HR/Sp02 (which I dont trust either) wearables. The tech just isnt there yet - unless of course you pay top dollar. Even then, its going to be off. Now if consistently off by the same number- not these radical jumps - then I would give it a better review with these caveats. But for anyone who has “borderline” conditions and Orthostatic Intolerance (OI) and POTS, its not even consistent enough to count on for record tracking and health management.
Guess I am going to have to keep up with the tried and true equipment I have calibrated at home. Oh well….

review_text:
Here is a 100% honest review. Forgive me if I gush over these buds, but I really am in heaven with them!

DISCLOSURE: I do not own a Samsung phone and have no intention of using them for streaming or with fitness apps. I purchased them solely to use in stand-alone mode, using a PC to upload music files (I use m4a files purchased on iTunes).

I use these buds for cycling round the city and working out at the gym. As I'm using the onboard memory rather than a phone, the battery life is totally fine for my purposes. The maximum time it takes for me to cycle anywhere is 30-40 minutes. Working out in the gym is about 90 mins. As I don't have a Samsung phone I can't check the battery level, but I can say that they haven't run out once. Based on the specs it should be 3 hours on one charge, and the charging capsule is very compact and easy to carry/use.

As for sound quality, I'm not sure why others are giving it bad reviews. I've spent thousands on high-end headphones, and I'm really impressed with these. The headphones I previously used in the gym were PowerBeats2, which I really didn't like. The sound from the IconX wipes the floor with the Beats, partly due to simply having a far better fit and better sound blocking. I found that the response was crisp and detailed, with a balanced sound. Even at low volume, I was able to enjoy the music in the gym without any external distractions. The powerbeats are leaky, sloppy and muddy by comparison.

What else to say? They're lightweight, well made, perform well and a joy to use, and I only really use one of its many functions. If you want something that will last 8 hours, then you simply won't find it in this form factor. If you need all the bells and whistles, then the battery life will be compromised. If, however, you just want a top notch, discreet music listening experience that you can use even during vigorous exercise, then don't hesitate. They are fantastic for what they were designed for!

review_title: Great Sound, Great Functionality, Short Battery Life
review_text:
The IconX Cordfree earbuds are an outstanding workout and travel companion. I've used them for workouts at home and on the road, and found that they performed every task I expected of them, with the only downside being how quickly the battery depletes.

Initial pairing and setup is simple with the Gear app. Once paired, I only lost connection one time over multiple uses, and that was easily resolved by putting the earbuds in the case to reset. The app can be used to load music onto the earbuds' internal memory, and control other settings (like which earbud is the primary).

Once paired, the earbuds work like any other bluetooth device. A touch-sensitive panel on the outside can be used to answer calls, skip tracks, pause music, and adjust volume. It took me a little while to master those controls because I put the earbuds in at a bit of an angle, and couldn't remember which direction was "up."

Overall comfort was good, once I found the correct inserts for my big ears. The earbuds stayed in with no difficulty through multiple vigorous HIIT workouts. Sound quality was excellent, and volume was more than sufficient to drown out ambient sounds in the gym. I do not recommend listening to music while running outside (because of the loss of situational awareness), but the earbuds do have an option - through the Gear app - for passing through ambient sounds. It seemed to help a little, but I still would still use them with caution anywhere that safety might be an issue.

The heart rate monitor is awesome. I'm not a fan of the Samsung Fitness app, but it paired with my HIIT Timer app (from the Google Play store) as a Bluetooth hear monitor, and did a fantastic job of tracking my heartrate throughout my workouts. That feature alone makes the earbuds worth it to me.

All in all, the Gear IconX earbuds do everything they set out to do. The only downside is battery life. If your workout/run lasts longer than an hour and a half, don't expect the earbuds to last. Fortunately they do charge quickly, with even a brief charge enough to get them to last a 30-minute workout. I'm not sure that the form factor would allow for any longer battery life using current technology, so I did not deduct a star for that issue. Everything else about the earbuds exceeded my expectations, and the heart rate monitor was especially nifty.

If you don't they just keep dropping the connection. Basically the loop has to be facing upwards in you ear. Any other position; well they won't work. So once I got that resolved; I discovered many other nice aspects of these. I like the ambient sound feature you can turn on or off and I really like the internal hard drive that you can store you music on the buds themselves instead of playing music from the phone. I didn't think I'd like that feature at first but after I tried it, I really do love it. I even retract my views about the controls. I think after one think fell into place; pretty much every thing else did as well. While they take some getting used to, once you master how they work, it actually pretty intuitive to use. All that said i raise my rating to 3 and 1/2 to 4 stars. The biggest downside is the battery life. The battery actually starts draining as soon as you remove from the case and put in you ears. You don't have to be listening to anything or having a call or anything. Once remove from the case, they are considered on rather in you ear or not. So good start for this technology from Samsung. I'm still pissed about the Galaxy Note 7 fiasco, but the earbuds get a pass for now!

review_title: I was impressed at how everything came together nicely. I assumed they would
review_text:
Ok. Here we go. They arrived this afternoon, 6 hours ago. 2 hours later, the indicator lights on the charging case were green, stating they were fully charged. I downloaded the Samsung Gear App and synched everything up. Initially, I was impressed at how everything came together nicely. I assumed they would. I'm on a GalaxyS6Edge and they're also a Samsung product. Its one of the reasons i chose this model over others. I went through the settings, turned off all the notifications as i didn't want interruptions while listening to my audiobook. I adjusted the unit volume and verified batteries were full in the app.
1 hour later:
* the app showed the batteries un-evenly down to half on the left and 2/5 on the right (right was the primary sync with the phone so i assumed it would go faster.
* the left earbud was constantly sending out notifications and disconnecting. The fit was actually decent so i didn't feel the need to swap out the gels. I'd removed them and re-inserted as the instructions suggested to re-sync and that would last a minute or two before the notifications/beeping would start again. I unpaired and re-paired, no change.
* on 3 occasions, both buds lost connection with the phone, despite being within 2 ft of it.

Those are my functional complaints with the device. I also have concerns for people who decide to look into this model for themselves. I've already packed it up for a refund so it aids me none.
* The charging case does not magnetically hold the buds in place when lined for charging. When you close the lid over the buds, the top pushes the buds down against the charging buttons/pins and that's when it begins. If the hinge ever breaks on the case, you're done for. The case is also plastic, be ware.
* The fit and look were fine, but i never felt confident it would hold.
* Instructions say to avoid touching the heart rate monitor pad on the buds when inserting in your ear to prevent mis-readings when synched up for activities. Its a small personal grudge but i don't want to have to think about how i'm holding them to get them in, i just wanna pop the buds in and go.

Advice: Avoid these earbuds... at least until they work out the kinks, improve the battery life and get a better charging method/case. As much as i love my Bragi, they have their own batch of issues. I do feel despite their issues, i still like them better than these IconX earbuds.

review_text: Yes I meant to give these five stars. For the right applications these are great. There are instrinsic design limitations wireless headset/fitness tracker of this size/fromat. I have over ear, noise canceling Bose headphones for when I plan to be listening for hours , taking business conference calls or going on a plane trip. However the Bose units don't fit in my pocket ( in a slightly larger than a pack of tic tack/gum/ Zippo lighter case). There are bluetooth headphones with longer battery life that sit on the back of your neck or have ear pieces connected by a cord - Ive tried and dislike both as they are uncomfortable and even short cords can still get in the way. None of the other headphones I own / have tried include the onboard fitness tacker function the IconX includes. In my experience Iconx run effectively for about 90 minutes continuous use before needing a recharge. If you're a hard core gym user, spending 90+ minutes at gym these arent for you. However if your workouts/runs  are less than 90 minutes , there are big advantages with these. The onboard music storage is great if you don't plan on taking a phone. If you are streaming from phone and get a call, the mic pick up is pretty good for conversation.  In practice I find tIconx usable all day, kept in my pocket with case/charger using them for mutliple 45-60 minutes sessions. If I'm working/listening for longer sessions I Bose units I keep in laptop bag.  While wired headphones for certain applications have major advantages there are times when wires are a pain and  these headphone ( even with their design limits) are so much better. If your budget means you need a single " multi application" head phone set - these are not right for you. If you budget allows you to have multiple headphones for different applications dont be overly put off by some of the negative reviews for these headphones. For walking, running, some comutes and gym visits ( 60-90 minutes) these may work out great for you. Is the onbaord fitness tracker useful or do you have that already on a band device? Remember than while the single use limit is probably 60-90 minutes , these will recharge in their case in your pocket or bag ( the case itself recharge on a "cell phone style" micro usb cable at home, at your desk or if you carry a battery back up. These earbuds will be a game changer for you. If you are active, work out, or enjoy running, these will make all of that more enjoyable. Below are a few of the qualities that you may be looking for in your future cord free earbuds.

Comfort:
Many cord free headphones tend to fall out of your ear or don’t fit right, making them uncomfortable. These headphones come with three different wingtip size options, so there is likely a size for your ear. The ear tip protrudes out of the earbud and fits comfortably into your ear. Once the earbuds are set in your ear, they are hardly noticeable once you begin your activities. They are a very lightweight design and will not fall out of your ear if they are placed correctly.

Sound Quality:
The sound quality is excellent. It can connect through Bluetooth on your phone or you can download music onto the earbuds through your computer. Each earbud has its own memory and once turned on, they synchronize. This feature allows you to perform your activity without being attached to your phone. They are also noise canceling but also protect your ears and warn you when the volume is being raised too high.

Touch Controls:
You can control your music all from just touching the earbuds. Swiping up and down on the side increases and decreases the volume. Double tapping the side of the earbuds allows you to skip to the next song and triple tapping allows you to replay the song that you just listened to. These touch control features are extremely convenient, especially when you are in the middle of performing an activity or do not have your phone nearby. When you are connected to Bluetooth through your earbuds, you are also able to answer or decline phone calls by simply tapping the side of the earbud.

Battery Life:
These earbuds come with a case that doubles as a charger. You can play your music library up to 3.4-3.8 hours or stream for 1.5-1.6 hours without charging. When the battery is running low, the headphones will give you an advanced notice before they run out. The portable charging case comes with a cord that you can plug into a phone charger adapter, making it easy to charge anywhere.

The Gear Icon Earbuds will be your perfect workout partner and the price is very reasonable considering the quality.

review_text:
With a simple earbud tip modification, the Samsung IconX earbuds are a game-changer. Here’s my experience with them after one week.

I’ve been using many different earbuds over the years - Bose, Samsung, Apple, Sennheiser, Sony, etc., and am active in the gym every day, putting any earbuds through hell. Biggest reason I wanted to try these is for freedom of the cord - I can't tell you how many times I've accidentally ripped earbuds out of my ears in the gym or while running. It's infuriating, but those days are GONE.

The Samsung IconX's are a valiant 1st Gen effort by Samsung.

EASY MODIFICATION (see pictures):
Let’s go through this first. For me, the basic provided rubber earbud tips always seem to put pressure on my eardrums, which is very uncomfortable and can be painful. Also, I can never seem to get a great seal, so all low-end frequencies are non-existent most of the time. The only time I could get a somewhat full sound with the provided earbud tips was while laying down doing push-ups - probably because of the way they were situated. Once I stood up, they lost all sound quality.

So, I purchased the [[ASIN:B002NUJ2RM Comply Premium Replacement Foam Earphone Earbud Tips - Isolation T-400 (Black, 3 Pairs, Medium)]], and modified them slightly to match the original earbud tip size. The material of these earbud tips allows for MUCH better sound isolation and frequency response. I cut 1/8" off each with a razor blade (very easy to cut through) and popped them on. NIGHT AND DAY difference. I could now hear the full spectrum and the seal was almost perfect. You'll have to experiment with what size works for you, but Medium seems to have done the trick. Sounds isolation is greatly improved with these as well, so you can focus on the music without effort. Also, they don't fit quite as nicely in the charging case, but certainly good enough, and the case shuts fine with a little extra pressure. See images.

The IconX's are now worth keeping.

SOUND QUALITY:
This is an interesting one, because we're relying heavily on Bluetooth to handle everything. Surprisingly, after the above modification, the IconX's sound great. I've used them for 6 days in the gym, running, sleeping, working, etc. I'm hearing things that I haven't before using past earbuds, better high-end response than a few wired earbuds I have, but of course not close to a good pair of wired headphones. My current reference headphones are my [[ASIN:B0016MNAAI beyerdynamic DT 770 Pro 80 ohm Studio Headphones]], and, while the IconX can't compete with these, I'm surprised on how well they handle certain low frequencies after modification. I do hear distortion at higher volumes, and I do wonder what type of compression is involved, as it competes with the music sometimes, but it's subtle enough to disregard.

BUILD QUALITY:
Impressive. These have a nice weight to them, no moving/loose parts, and fit nice and snug in the provided charging case. The overall shape seems to wok very well with most ears, so I think Samsung has done a nice job here.

BATTERY LIFE:
Just OK. Yesterday, I used them (fully charged) in the gym for about an hour and fifteen minutes, and they started to die. It'd be nice to get a solid two hours out of them while connected to bluetooth.

SOFTWARE:
Limited right now. One gripe I have is that the IconX's won't recognize folders of music in the internal storage that I've copied over. They force you to just dump songs in one main music folder. This needs to be fixed with a software update. I really need to be able to organize my music by playlists, so when I'm running I can listen to certain songs at tempo, etc. So, I'm not really happy with the way music is stored internally. Maybe I'm missing something?

TOUCH CONTROLS:
Overall these work very well - they're just too big. It's very easy to advance the song, raise volume by swiping either direction, pause songs, etc. But, due to how large the touch surface is, it's very easy to accidentally send a command without wanting to. For instance, if I take one out really quick to talk to someone, it usually causes me to accidentally pause or skip a track. This can be frustrating, but I think Samsung could possibly issue a software/firmware update to allow users to lessen the active touch area. I think if they reduced it by 30%, it would be easier to manage accidental commands.

PROS:
Complete, wireless freedom
Great sound quality (with above modification)
Build quality and solid construction
Price - I actually think $199 is pretty reasonable for 1st Gen
Charging case - works perfectly, and can charge the earbuds several times

CONS:
Battery life when connected to Bluetooth
Touch pad is too large and sensitive
Provided earbud tips degrade sound quality
No playlist configuration - can't save folders

OVERALL VERDICT:
There's so many good things going with these, and once you realize that you have completely wireless music, you'll wonder why you've been dealing with cords all this time. It's really a game-changer. I'd recommend to buy them, along with the above Comply Earbuds Tips, and put them through some their paces. I bet you won't look back. I haven't tried The Dash by Bragi, but with the IconX's being $100 less, it was an easier decision to make.

Four stars. Samsung should provide additional foam earbud tips (like many other companies) so people like me don't possibly give up on them too quickly. Also, I'd recommend Samsung really work on updating the music-organization software to allow users to use playlists. We have to have these.

Thanks, Samsung for a really great product. They're with me wherever I go.

review_text:
These are far better than I expected them to be. To begin with, I have no interest in the health features. My interest was in active noise cancelling and sound quality in a great form factor and these deliver.

As another reviewer mentioned, these seal the ear canal so you will hear a thumping as you walk, run, or do any activity that is jarring. This is one of the reasons Comply foam tips are so great. They seal the ear canal but because they are foam, air can escape so you don’t get the thumping. (it is equivalent to the pressure thumping you get in the car when you roll down just one window a crack)

Pros:
• Very comfortable, even after 2 hours (which is when the battery died)
• Great sound. Mostly mid-range but good bass and treble. They sounded better than the “gear circle” headphones I had and they are on par with many other higher end headsets. They sound as good as my 1st generation LG Tone Infinums.
• The capsule (charging case) is small and comfortable enough to carry in your pocket, purse, or bag.
• Charge quickly in the case.
• Comply foam tips fit but… (see cons)
• Active noise cancellation and you can manage that from the phone app
• Great phone app

Cons:
• Battery lasts only a couple of hours (about 2 on average in my experience)
• As I said, the Comply ear tips fit but then you can’t close them in the charging case with them on so you are left with three options:
o Forget the Complys and get the “thumps” from the standard tips if you are active
o Take them on and off between charging (ridiculous, too much work)
o Cut about 2-3 millimeters off the Comply foam tips so they will fit in the charging case (this is what I did and I am happy with this choice)
• When I use only on ear piece (audiobooks that are mono or if I’m using the phone). The signal cuts out a lot just by turning my head too far to the left or right if my phone is in my pocket.
o Interestingly, this does not happen at all if both headsets are in.

Final notes:
• Ambient sound is a great option for running or walking as you want to hear cars, etc. but you can turn it off so the active noise cancellation can cut out much of the noise of your lawn mower or blower.
• I cannot recommend these for air travelers as the battery won’t last more than 2 hours or so and it would be so easy to drop one and lose it.
Overall, happy with them

review_text: Let's get something straight here. These FITNESS earbuds were built for just that- fitness! They were not designed to be taken to work and last you a full 8-10 hr shift. If you still want more than 3hrs battery life for a workout, then you're either an Olympic athlete or overdoing it, I'm betting the latter. There's no reason to rate this amazing product poorly due to battery life; it gets the job done. As far as fitment, they fit better than the bragi dash, jaybird x2, jaybird freedom, jabra sports coach etc just to name a few. Sucks however, that there's no shuffle or playlist option so essentially you have one giant library of tracks set in one order. Also, iPhone users won't benefit much from these ear buds since you'd be missing out on about half of the features these bad boys can offer. Overall, a great product you won't be disappointed if your expectations are realistic and by realistic I mean don't hope for a 10 hr battery life.

review_title: Great watch, very pretty! Just a few minor flaws
review_text:
Bought this watch a few weeks ago as I've never had a smart watch before and didn't want to start with a super expensive one (I'm learning the ropes first!). This is a good starter watch and it's very pretty! Short list of pros and cons:

Pros:
- It's gorgeous and I love that you can customize the face. I made my own cherry blossom face for spring and it's so pretty!
- I like the sleep tracker, and the fact that you can download the data onto your phone.
- You can view messages and app notifications on your watch (although you can't reply back).
- The raise-to-wake function is cool, that way I don't drain the battery. It only turns on the clock face when you're looking at it.
- The battery power is really good! Mine lasted three weeks without a single charge.
- The step counter is handy, and you can set a goal for yourself.
- The 'find phone' function is awesome and I've used it numerous times!
- I can start and pause and skip music from the music interface.

Cons:
- The weather function doesn't work correctly (on mine at least). It only updates once in the morning and then stays the same the rest of the day. Yesterday it was 90F and my watch read 66F all day.
- The watch is a bit large for my small wrist. I got a round watch because rectangular ones are definitely too big, but it still feels really large.
- The watch disconnects a lot, even if I just leave my phone on the counter and walk upstairs for something. It'll immediately break the connection. Then I have to resync it again via the app. Not hard to do, but that means my messages don't come through and the 'find phone' function doesn't work (which is unhandy when the whole point of finding your phone is that you lost it, so you obviously can't sync it!).

All in all I'm pretty happy with it, and it's possible that my issues don't happen to everyone. It's a great watch for health tracking (including periods!) and sleep tracking.

review_text:
To be honest, I almost sent this watch back the first day. So far, I'm glad I did not.
Packaging: cute; easy to open(unlike Barbies in the 90's)
Set up: extremely easy. Pairing was a breeze, the app is free.
Upon downloading the app and selecting English for the language, it became very apparent that the app was not designed by someone fluent in English. This was my main reason for considering sending it back. However, while some of the phrasing is a bit silly, it is not very difficult to decipher the meaning of different features, and none of the actual watch features have this issue. It is only the app itself that has a slight language barrier.
My favorite feature: "raise to wake." You can adjust the time parameters; during the hours you are normally awake, the screen turns on when you lift the watch towards yourself, and during the hours you are normally asleep, the screen stays off no matter how much you move around.
Second favorite feature: water resistance. I wore this while swimming in the ocean(not diving) and had no issues.
Third favorite feature: the battery life!! I've been wearing this watch for a week straight and the only time I've charged it was for approximately 5 minutes immediately after unboxing.

Heart rate monitor is not extremely accurate during exercise, but what can you really expect from a topwear watch?

Overall, I decided to keep this watch because it fulfills my desire for a fitness watch and also a good looking timepiece without breaking the bank. It is comfortable, stylish, and works well for my level of need.

review_title: The screen is great when you learn how to use it in different environments.
review_text:
First, once you figure out how to properly use it, the display is good (I'll explain a little further down). I was trying to decide between this and a Microsoft Band 2 which has a great screen and more or less the same features. With the vivoactive HR I can synch to Apple's health app (works great) and Garmin has a decent selection of apps, widgets and watch faces that I can add and many are customizable. I have been very impressed with their library of add-on tools. The heart rate has appeared spot on, I've tested it against the same model pulse oximeter my doctor uses and they normally match, even after exercise. The notifications are great. I get several pages related to work every day and if I am some place I don't want to pull my phone out, I can glance at the messages, tap the ones I want to read the full text on and then clear them if I am done. I wear a Bluetooth earpiece a lot and I can answer a call on the watch and the earpiece will pick it up. Saves me from fumbling around my ear for a button or giving a voice command to answer. This is great if you are excusing yourself from a meeting to take a call.
Now back to the screen. I first used it in a dimly lit room and I though at first the other reviewers we right. But after adjusting the brightness and learning the best angles for viewing it is great! Outside is stupendous. Very clear, very crisp. In the dark it is great because the backlight isn't overly bright (I'm not trying to use it like a light source to find something) but it is bright enough to read everything easily on the screen. Readability was my one qualm going in based on the reviews, but my experience has showed that if you learn the best ways to read it in various lighting conditions you will not be let down. It also has enough cool features that my inner geek is very happy. When I read the reviews that were comparing this to other bands in the same price range, almost all said this was the model that integrated all the features they wanted very nicely. I highly recommend the vivoactive HR, it's performance and features have not let me down. After three solid days of use, including some GPS usage, my battery is only down to 70%. I think I believe the 8 day battery life claim. Enjoy it, it is a great fitness tool and smart watch!

review_text:
Any review on a product is going to be based on the reviewer's biases and unique expectations for the product. What I have to say may or may not be meaningful to you, depending on how your usage compares to mine.

I purchased my Vivoactive HR in November 2017 and was excited to get a GPS watch that would track my jogging and biking. I'm above the normal age of retirement, so both of those have been sporadic, especially during the winter months here in Chicago.

I found the Vivoactive HR easy to set up and immediately enjoyed seeing my jog and biking distances and pace recorded. It served as a motivator to keep at it, especially as I was able to detect progress in my times, distance and the lowering of my heart rate. As others have noted, the ability of the watch to accurately detect my stairs usage has been consistently disappointing, to the point that long ago I stopped expecting it to track it.

I would probably still be satisfied with my Vivoactive HR but for two factors. First, I accidentally scratched the lens. Yeah, I should have used a screen protector. That was mainly a cosmetic flaw that, while annoying, hasn't really impacted the watch's performance. The second factor I discovered in the middle of a bike ride, when I realized that the watch was basically coming loose from the housing. I was concerned that I'd be out for a jog or a ride and lose the entire mechanism without realizing it.

At that point I had two choices. I could send the watch in for repair and pay more money than the watch was worth or I could attempt to secure it myself. I chose the latter, and let's just say that it didn't turn out so great. I still wear the watch, but the ability to swipe from one screen to the next has become very cumbersome so for the most part I just use it to tell time and to check notifications as they come in.

There are more features that I have not commented on, and won't for the purpose of this review. Obviously, there are newer Vivoactive models out there, so I don't know how pertinent this will be for anyone. I haven't decided if I will purchase another GPS watch, but if I decide to, based on my experience with the HR, I will likely buy another Garmin. If you are just dipping your toe into the whole GPS watch scene and can find a used HR in good shape for a great price, I would recommend it.

review_text:
My first VAHR worked for two years and promptly died. Is it perfect for my needs - no, but it is the best option out there. I just ordered another one.

Pro
1. I like the style - not this huge sports watch - and fits my small wrist well.
2. Price point is good - no need to spend $500 + on a watch. This has nearly all the same functions
3. Waterproof - truly waterproof. I do water sports and have never had a problem.
4. Battery life. I once was able to keep the watch going (i turned it off at night) for almost a week, recording activiites every day.
5. Interchangeable bands (cosmetic i know, but fun nonetheless)
6. Heart rate monitor on the wrist seems to be pretty good, although nothing compares to the chestband.
7. Connects well with the Garmin software. Does not have to be connected to your phone to record activities.

Cons
1. Mine died after two years. I mean completely died.
2. About a year in, it was incredibly glitchy in charging. At the end, I couldn't click the watch into the charger, but rather had to precisely balance it to enable it to charge. Even cleaning the watch really well, as well as the charger, didn't help. This was a progressive problem.
3. The heart rate monitor (wrist) is iffy for those of us with smaller wrists. I had to be careful with how I put the watch on, otherwise the HR function wouldn't work (position - above the wrist bone, and a bit tighter than I would prefer). Other sports watches i have had, have not had this problem. This seems to be specific to the design of the watch.
4. Impossible to use the touch screen when fingers are wet. (challenge for those of us who do water sports)
5. Not able to program workouts from computer and then sync to watch.
6. Hard to toggle between time and ongoing activity as the touchscreen isn't very responsive when your fingers are wet. (I honestly don't see anyway to fix this)
7. Unable to remove all the golf stuff from the phone. (I appreciate the option, but those of us who aren't into golf, it would be nice to move those activities out of the queue)

Like I said, I'm overall happy with this. I think it is a good entry point into the Garmin sport watch. The HR wrist option is a nice add and I like the design and functionality.

review_title: The best Activity Tracker/GPS  Garmin ever produced!!
review_text:
09/04/16 UPDATE: Vivoactive HR is now connected to my Varia Rerview Radar! The Vivoactive while plugged in, has some software updates that I wasn't aware of and now it started showing warning when vehicles approach from behind just like my Garmin Explorer 1000. Many people complained that the Garmin 1000 beeped when detect cars from behind, but the sound was too tiny to hear. Well, the Vivoactive actually beeps a little louder and vibrates when the Varia detects cars coming up. This will get you to look at your Garmin! So if you have same set up as mine with Varia Rearview Radar and Garmin Edge 1000, you may want to consider the Vivoactive HR. With the warning, I am sure it helps make you safer while riding in the streets and highways. Solid five-star product!

I have most things Garmin: car GPS, bike GPS, wrist GPS, speed + cadence and Varia rearview radar for my bike. I have tried several Garmin activity trackers, but returned them as they did not meet my expectations, either display unreadable or too small for my wrist (vivosmart), so I tried the Vivoactive HR with a lot of skepticisms.

First impression: this is probably the best looking GPS/activity tracker Garmin ever produced. The device is light and at perfect size; not too small that you it is hard to read line Garmin’s Vivosmart and not too big like others from Garmin. I usually wear a Large for other activity trackers, but for this Vivoactive, a regular size fit me perfect. There are only 2 sizes for the band: Regular and XL. The band is made of large, soft and textured rubber; so soft and nice that you wonder how long would it last. After two days wearing it, I think it will last a long time if not abused.

Screen is a little bit dimmed for my taste, but total readable under sunlight. I wear it on my Saturday bike ride to test it out, and so far really like it. Background can be set to either white or black, I have mine set to white to improve contrast both indoor and outdoor. The Vivoactive synced up with satellites fairly quickly, it only takes less than a minute after I selected “Bike” to begin my ride. Yes, you have to select the activity as nothing (except now the unpopular Basis) does a good job in detecting what activity you are currently doing.

I have the Vivoactive HR connected with my iPhone, cadence and speed sensors on my bike. The manual said it would connect to Garmin Varia Rear view radar detector, but I could not find the option in its sensor page. I imagine it will vibrate to let me know if cars are coming form behind. Hopefully Garmin will release an upgrade for this soon. If you have a Garmin cycling GPS already, you probably don’t need to connect the speed and cadence sensors to see these statistic. But since Vivoactive HR can use these information to calculate calories burnt, it might be a good to after all.

The notification feature work flawlessly after I connected the Vivoactive HR to my phone. App notifications, text messages, WhatApps messages and phone calls all came through and display on the screen. It works so well that I consider turning this feature off while I ride! Music control works great too, you can either start your music from the phone or from Vivoactive, but keep in mind that you have more control starting from your phone and use the Vivoactive to skip, pause or go back.

There are many apps that can be loaded to the Vivoactive and more from Garmin’s IQ Store. I did not try this feature, as I don’t see the need for more apps. There are 4 watch faces that come with the Vivoactive, I chose “Traditional Digital” as I think it fit me most. While riding and Bike activity selected, you can only see speed, distance travel and elapse time.

To read the watch face in the dark, you only need to tap on the screen. Screen touch actually works the way it is supposed to, and I am pretty happy about that. review_text:
It's a great sport watch, but that's it. I've tracked about 200 miles of running with this watch and have worn it for over a year and a half. It can track for hours on end; I ran a half marathon in just under two hours and it recorded everything perfectly.

Pros:
*Very accurate GPS (can easily tell which side of the street you're on)
>consequently great at tracking steps and distance
*Very accurate heart rate monitor (count it yourself if you don't believe me)
*Had no issues with water. I've worn it swimming and in the shower everyday for over a year.
*Garmin's app tracks a LOT of information (cadence, running route, sleep patterns, HR zones, fastest times, avg. speed, fastest speed, etc.). The list is very long and the main reason I kept this watch for so long.
*Very durable. I've hit the screen pretty hard against concrete and walls and it held up just fine.
*

Cons:
*The HR monitor protrudes and does dig into your skin if your watch is too tight. It still reads your HR just fine when loose enough. Be sure to loosen it before you sleep.
*The sensitivity of the watch is very small. The touchscreen often won't work if your hands are sweaty.
*There is almost an entire second delay when using the touch screen, the biggest flaw on this watch in my opinion.
*Expect not to use many apps on this watch. The interface is meant for sports, not for features you might see on modern smart watches.

TL;DR
The best feature is Garmin's app. The GPS and HR monitor are very accurate and the durability is great. The HR monitor does protrude and can dig into your skin if too tight. Overall it's a good sport watch and it's reasonably priced. It's not meant to have many features beyond sports.

I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who doesn't run though; it's mainly what this watch is built around imo.

review_text:
<Update 11/27/2016: My wife and I have now had the VivoActive HR for 5 months. We still love the watch. I wanted to complement Garmin on their customer service. My watch bricked after jumping into a mountain lake over the summer. It went completely black screen and wouldn't power up. I called Garmin Customer Service and they replaced it for free since it obviously failed to be water proof. It only took a week to send mine in and get a new one back.>

I did not order these from Amazon. My wife and I each got a Vivoactive HR, we ordered directly from Garmin. We have now had them for a week and I will update this review if need be. I use mine to track steps, biking and snowboarding next season. The built in altimeter was a big selling point. I have the previous Vivoactive. It does not have an altimeter. So you can use it to track ski/snowboard runs but it uses GPS flat speed and not your actual 3d speed. The new one can now do that. My wife uses hers for running.
I read a few reviews were people had issues with going out of range of their phone and then coming back in range and the watch not automatically re-connecting via Bluetooth to their phone. My wife and I spent some time testing that and we could not reproduce the same results. Our watches re-connected every time we came back in range of our phone.

Initial Setup:
We did not have any issues out of the box or connecting to the Garmin Connect App on our iPhones. Like the instructions state, pair the device directly through the Connect App. We both also used the Garmin Express desktop app during the initial charge to customize what apps and widgets are installed and in what order they appear as you swipe through the interface. I deleted all the apps I wouldn’t use, like indoor biking, rowing, Stand Up Paddle Boarding etc to make the screens easier to navigate. Like any Garmin device it is important to take the time to go through all the settings to tweak and customize it to what you want.

Screen:
Let’s address the elephant in the room. The screen, which seems to be the cause of many of the 1 star reviews. I can understand how this can happen. All the marketing material show the screen bright and very readable. However this screen is designed for battery life and to be read out doors. When in direct light it is super bright and easy to read. However in low light without the backlight on it is hard to read. Straight out of the box the backlight is set to level 3, which is hard to see. My Vivoactive HR came out of the box with the new 2.4 update installed. So I was immediately able to navigate the settings menu to turn the backlight from level 3 to level 6 and it was plenty bright. It does go up to 9 and is VERY bright. My wife’s did not have the update. But during the first sync with her phone the update installed. Once you can adjust the backlight the screen is fine. We did not have any backlight bleed like some have mentioned. I think many of other reviewer’s issues are just their expectations were not met. This watch is purpose built to be an activity tracker with some Smartwatch functions built in. It isn’t an Apple Watch, but then again it has standalone GPS, altimeter, compass, heart rate and other sensors built in, and does not have to be charged every night.

Step and Activity Tracking:
Step tracking has been flawless for both of us. It is accurate, including counting floors. I tested in my house going from the first floor to the second floor and it seems to track just fine. Sometimes there was a delay between showing the floor counted, but it would show up. As for activity tracking, it has been outstanding. It is easy to start, stop and view data while tracking the activity. It also uploads to the Garmin Connect really fast. I can say the sync / upload on this Vivoactive is faster than the first gen. I have used it to track mountain biking and walking so far. My wife has used it to track running with no issues.

Heart Rate:
Here I feel is another elephant, sitting in the room eating peanuts. Let’s remember that this is optical HR. It shines a light on your wrist. It isn’t going to be 100% accurate. There are many factors. Placement, hair on your arm, heck even a mole where your band sits could cause issues. It isn’t going to work for strength training, weightlifting etc. My personal experience has been it is mostly accurate while not exercising. There were a few times where I could tell it wasn’t right, like saying my HR was at 85 when sitting. My RHR is about 58. But it only lasted for a min or too, and knowing what my HR should be I could call it what it was, an outlier. I wasn’t too worried about it. During activity tracking I had no issue and it seemed to stay accurate the whole time while on my mountain bike. It was great to be able see the correlation between steep technical climbs and the increase in my HR. There was a point on my ride where HR didn’t work so well, but that is because the watch moved a bit. That was my fault, I didn’t tighten it enough.

Look / Fit / Comfort:
I love the look of this one. My old Vivoactive looked clunky, unsophisticated and would not fit in well with business attire. The new one looks fine from the morning jog, to the afternoon meeting with clients. The new band is also an improvement. This one is more comfortable than the old one for sure. I can wear it all day just fine.

Battery Life:
The battery lasted 6 days, with 3 GPS tracked activities. I have now turned off the heart rate monitor to save battery life. I don’t really care about 24 hour HR monitoring. I turn it on when I am going to track an activity, and turn it off after. That will probably improve battery life even more.

Final thoughts
My wife and I love this watch and I gave it 5 stars. If I had to pick a flaw it would be that it has the same amount of screen real-estate as the old one but with more resolution and flipped into landscape. From the pictures I thought the screen would be bigger than the previous generation. I do like the new orientation and higher resolution. I would recommend this to anyone who lives an active lifestyle.

review_title: Excellent all-around watch for runners general activity tracking
review_text:
After owning a couple of Pebble watches, I was looking for a more dedicated fitness tracker that can also do simple phone alerts. While I'm not a marathon runner or even what I'd consider a super serious runner (yet!), I wanted something more than just a general step tracker, and was looking for a device that could accurately track runs, walks, biking, and other activity while monitoring my heart rate. The Vivoactive HR was the perfect choice.

Being a Garmin, the GPS tracking of runs, walks, or bike rides is perfect. And the non-GPS tracking of steps and indoor runs has continued to get more accurate as the device learns my stride length, etc. The ability to customize the apps and widgets with only the activities I do, or add apps for things like 7 minute workouts is great. The Garmin Connect app for iOS makes it relatively easy to install and remove apps, and the watch stays connected and sync'd to the app consistently. I have had a few little issues with iOS push notifications sometimes coming through multiple times (certain emails seem to pop back up on the watch every so often) and I haven't quite figure out if I have some settings tweaking to do or if there's a software bug. It's not so often as to be incredibly annoying though. After all, I bought this as an activity tracker first and a smart watch second.

I don't really do the community fitness thing so I can't speak to how the Garmin Connect community features work but if you're in to sharing and comparing workouts with friends, it's in there. I also haven't found the perfect app to track weight lifting but, I've been recording weight lifting as a basic cardio activity and at least then I can track things like heart rate, and when I did sessions, etc.

The heart rate monitor has been covered in many reviews and seems to be as accurate as a wrist based HR monitor can be. I don't have any chest straps to compare it to but I haven't noticed anything wildly off and based on other review comparisons (DC Rainmaker especially), it seems to be accurate enough.

Goals (steps, floors climbed, intensity minutes, etc) can be set manually or the watch and app will adjust based on your activity. I've been letting Garmin set my goals and it's definitely gotten me moving to meet each day's goal. That was exactly the motivation I needed.

I don't regularly wear the watch to sleep but I did a few times and it seemed to track my sleep as well as any other competitor.

Overall, I am very happy with this watch's performance and how it's immediately fit into my fitness routine.

review_title: All-around activity tracker with golf features and good battery life? YES
review_text:
I want to start this off by saying that this is the first fitness tracker I have owned. I would consider myself an athlete and have been one for basically my entire life. The sports I've played have changed over the years, but I've always been pretty active. I looked at other devices in the past like Fitbit, Polar, Nike, and even other Garmin devices, and nothing was appealing enough for me to finally buy into the whole activity tracking craze. A few months back, a friend showed me his Garmin Vivosmart HR during a volleyball tournament and showed me everything you can do with the Garmin Connect app. I play a lot of volleyball, so I was also a little concerned about wearing something on my wrist while playing since you pass with your arms, but he claimed that he didn't really notice it while playing. The Garmin ecosystem seemed pretty cool, so I decided to jump on Amazon and search for something for myself.

I landed on the Vivoactive HR. Unfortunately, this was in March and it hadn't been released yet. Because of this, I wasn't able to find many hands on reviews. But the feature set had everything I was looking for. The main features I was looking for were activity tracking, sleep tracking, wrist-based heart rate sensor, built-in GPS, and decent battery life. The golf features and touchscreen were added bonuses. I golf a couple times a month during the warmer months of the year, and having a rangefinder on my wrist seemed pretty convenient. So I ordered it way back in March, but I didn't receive it until May 2. However, shortly after receiving mine, I noticed that the screen seemed to be crooked. It was like the display (under the glass) was turned slightly counterclockwise. I ended up calling Garmin directly and arranging for a replacement to be sent out. They sent one while allowing me to keep my current Vivoactive HR which I would send back when receiving the new one. After receiving the new one, I saw that the screen was mounted correctly. I will note that the device itself seemed to function normally otherwise except for one small problem which I will note later when talking about golf.

APPS AND FEATURES:

Heart Rate Monitoring: So I've had this thing for about 3 weeks now. I feel like for the price point it is at, it is truly awesome. Heart rate monitoring seems to be pretty accurate. I am not the type of person to care about perfectly exact HR numbers, but I've measured my pulse by feel and it seems to be pretty close. It does seem like doing things (like weightlifting) where you are tensing up your forearm does seem to mess with the HR sensor a bit, but it's not bad enough for me to really complain about.

Step Counter: The step counter appears to be fairly accurate. I am not too concerned about it being perfect. I just use it to get an idea of how much I've actually been on my feet any given day. I have noticed that it doesn't seem to count as many steps as I think it would when I am mowing the lawn with a push mower. Not a huge deal but a little disappointing. Otherwise it seems to keep track of my step count pretty well.

Sleep Tracking: Sleep tracking is neat. In my experience, the Vivoactive HR does a solid job of figuring out when I fall asleep and when I wake up. I am a little bit skeptical about the periods of "light sleep" and "deep sleep" that it records in the Garmin Connect app. Also, it doesn't always seem to see when I wake up during the night. I know that I woke up to go to the bathroom the other night and it didn't seem to notice the movement at all. You'd think if it saw steps in the middle of the night, it would assume you are awake. I will say that it has picked up other times that I've simply woke up in bed and fallen back asleep, but it doesn't seem to be perfect in this regard. Nonetheless, I am happy that it seems to pick up on when I'm actually falling asleep and waking up every night.

Activity Tracking: The only activities I've played with so far are walking, running, and a custom activity that I created for volleyball. I only use the GPS for walking and running, and it has been very accurate. Also, it has never taken more than a few seconds to get a good GPS lock. It's just nice to have GPS because I'd rather have my distance/pace calculated based on something accurate like GPS as opposed to the activity tracker counting your steps and estimating your stride distance. It's also really nice not having to take my phone with me to use GPS.

Golf features: As I said before the golf features were an added bonus. I downloaded some local courses and have used the golf app a few times now. The yardages have been accurate for the three courses that I have played. The app itself will show you distance to the hole when the pin is in front, middle, or back of the green. It will show you yardages to doglegs and layups. You can also measure the distance of your shots if you are into that kind of thing. You can even see (albeit primitive) the layout of the green on one of the screens. I did run into one problem with the golf app. On the layup screen, numbers would occasionally go "missing". There was a par 5 where I know it was about 150 yards to layup to 100 yards out, and the screen would display 50 instead of 150. This seemed to happen fairly often, and since I was familiar with the courses I was playing, it wasn't a big deal. But I called Garmin about it anyway, and they were actually able to reproduce it. They said that a software update should fix it. A new software version came out just the other day, so I will try it again this weekend and report back if it is fixed.

THE OTHER STUFF:

Battery life: For something that has a decent sized display and 24/7 HR monitoring, I think the Vivoactive HR has great battery life. Obviously if you are a heavy GPS user, the battery will drain much faster than normal. I charged to 100% just over 5 days ago, and none of the workouts I've done in the last 5 days have required GPS. I'm currently sitting at 50%. I guess if you go off this, you should get about 10 days of battery without GPS usage. During my last 25-minute run with GPS on, the battery level dropped about 2-3% which didn't seem unreasonable. Golf appears to suck the most out of the battery since GPS is turned on for a few hours at a time. During a normal 18-hole round (a little over 4 hours) with GPS on the whole time, the battery percentage dropped by about 20%. I know the Vivoactive HR is rated for about 8 days without GPS and 13 hours with GPS on. So the battery actually appears to perform better than what it is rated for.

Touchscreen: I've seen the touchscreen readability as a topic of debate on some other websites. It is actually more readable in direct sunlight than in any other circumstances. It is very readable with normal indoor lighting. It is impossible to read in the dark unless you have the backlight on. In most situations, I don't really feel like I need the backlight. But it does its job when it is needed. The screen isn't the highest resolution thing you'll ever seen, but it still looks nice. The touchscreen is responsive and accurately responds to touches, and I feel like it has actually gotten more responsive and fluid with the latest update.

Comfort, size, and looks: I have never worn watches. I was a little worried about having something on my wrist all day, every day...especially while sleeping and playing volleyball. After wearing the Vivoactive HR for a few days, I don't really even notice it anymore. I find it to be very comfortable. I can see how it might be too large for some people who are accustomed to wearing smaller activity trackers. But I think it's the price you pay for something that has a decent sized touchscreen with HR monitoring built in. I am wearing the version with the regular band (not XL), and I would say I have slightly smaller than average wrists for a guy. I wear it fairly tight and still have 9 notches to work with on the band. As far as looks go...you're not going to trick anyone into thinking it's some kind of luxury watch. It looks like an activity tracker, but I actually prefer the design over the design of the original Vivoactive. It still looks pretty sleek, and I have had a lot of people ask me about it. Also, I work in IT, so no one really cares if I'm wearing something real fancy looking. If you want to spruce things up a little bit, there are quite a few downloadable watch faces available, and the band can also be switched out.

Durability: This one is still up in the air. The Vivoactive HR is mostly plastic, but to me, it doesn't feel cheap. The two buttons underneath the screen feel pretty solid. I did buy a screen protector for the glass, but I haven't put it on yet. I'm debating whether or not I actually need to put it on. I have always taken care of my electronics, but I don't take most of my electronics running or play a volleyball tournament with them attached to my wrist. It feels like it will hold up, but I don't think I will truly have an idea for at least a few months.

Other stuff: The smart notifications feature works well. I am able to pick and choose what notifications I want relayed from my cell phone. You can't really do a whole lot with the notifications other than view them, but I have found that I actually look at my phone a lot less now because of this. The notifications turn off during your designated sleeping schedule, so they won't annoy you when you're lying in bed. However, the alarm feature has a strong enough vibration to wake me up every morning. This is nice because I no longer need to blare audio from the alarm on my cell phone and wake up my wife at the same time. Also, there are a decent amount of watch faces/apps/widgets available. So far I've only touched the watch faces, but it is nice that quite a bit can be customized to fit your needs.

Overall, I'm very happy with the Vivoactive HR. The reason I gave it 4 stars is because of the bugs in the golf app. I'm taking it out to the golf course a couple times this weekend, so I'll see if the update fixed the problem. If so, I may come back and re-rate it as 5 stars. And if I think of anything else I want to add in, I will do so.

review_title: Nearly as good as Apple watch for much less, many cool apps available free and low cost.  Quality product from GPS Giant Garmin.
review_text:
Intuitive, that's the first thing that came to mind with this watch. I have a golf watch and a high end exercise watch already from fast Vine purchases, and both of them were nice, but they had a moderately steep learning curve. I was checking back and forth with the manual or instructions to use them, if I put them down for a while, I'd have to relearn how to use them again. This watch is different from the moment I took it out of the box, I pushed a button on the bottom and I was taken through a quick set-up tutorial. In seconds I had the time GPS set, and was looking through the list of apps. I tested a few of the exercise apps for walking and the find my phone app. I'm not a great smart phone user, I've lived with a cheap 20 flip phone my friend got me at a Christmas gift exchange back in 2007. Bad sound, too small screen, some built in apps, but did not run on any common OS, predated iPhone and Android OS I believe. That is the reason I call this intuitive. I used my computer to go to the website instructed by the watch when I tried to access a WiFi needing app. It told me about the Garmin app, and so I fired up a BLU phone I got on Amazon with an Android OS, I've used it very little to date, not even activated the phone part yet save testing it with a friends GSM sim card. I went to the play store and in under 60 seconds had the app, and was pairing it with the watch, intuitive!

Function two buttons at the bottom and a touch screen. Can be seen in bright sunlight, I took it outside to allow the GPS to link easier. I knew to do that because my Garmin auto mapping GPS in my car usually needs a clear line of sight to the sky to initialize the GPS location system. When I paired the device to may BLU phone, the data was all transferred from my earlier set-up, a nice feature. Now something else fun and useful, widgets, I must log into my computer at least once or twice a day to check the weather for current temp and upcoming forecast. I scroll down to the weather widget and get all the weather info I usually need on the spot. The other widgets I use are the heart rate monitor, a constant update, the and a pedometer to see how long I walk during the day. All in sharp contrast, and in color, tap the screen for a back light at night, during the day it's easy to see in brightly lit conditions. There are new apps being developed for this as well, they are rated on the google play site. I don't have one, but I understand it has remote controls for camera's of various types based on a control technology. The music controls only work with you're downloaded MP3's from your Android Music App. Since there are developers working on this I can see where Pandora, and other music services both pay and free versions, may be linked in the future, but for now they are not, as far as I could find out. Again this was an easy if not intuitive thing to find on the watch. I also found it easy to use the directional thing to get back to your car at the mall or back to the right hotel in a big city. It's not a specialized app (although someone will eventually make one if it has a market), but you record your GPS coordinates, and the watch guides you back to the origin from whatever direction. It won't understand objects in the way or streets here, so remember it's for walking and you might have to adjust a little for obstructions. I didn't try the golf, and it's a nice feature, but I have a more elaborate watch made just for that. I may edit this later if I ever do a comparison, but if you don't have anything, this seems like a pretty good add on with all the other sports.

I've never seen an Apple watch yet, but I'm guessing this may not be quite that flexible, yet it doesn't cost two to five times as much either. I think it's the best compromise between Apple and something like Fit Bit for having a useful watch beyond telling the time.

Application Fun:

1. Weather Widget: Main screen gets you clouds/sun, high low temperature, percent precipitation, more button gets you next for hours of the same.
2. Heart Monitor: Gives current heart rate, high low, and resting heart rate charted with thin lines showing readings over 4 hour period. You can also find historical info for the last 7 days.
3. Calorie Counter: Counts Calories burned.
4. Steps: Tracks the number of steps you've taken over a given time period.
5. Music Controls: Has play/pause, volume up and down, tracks forward and reverse.
6. My Day: Tracks combinations of activity apps.
7. Lights: Couldn't explore much, but apparently control for bicycle lighting.
8. Biorhythm: A widget that tracks your daily biorhythm, I used to look at these a lot, cool way to track these.
9. Skywatch: It uses a lot of memory, but I had to do the skywatch app, cool to see how you can orient while looking at the sky to find various planets, the sun and the moon. It would be great paired with a telescope for someone new to planet star gazing.
10. Phone Finder: One of the first I loaded, it has a distinctive ring and flashes the camera flash LED for visual notification in the dark.

Dozens of others: Many with different watch faces or specialty things, even fishing cat and when you reach your fitness goal it gets it's fish.

I normally would have some downsides for this, but other then it needs memory expansion, since you may run it out of memory with all the great apps out there, I can't think of any. Maybe a bit more robust battery life, but it the watch mode it's pretty good so I've not complaining. Recommended for anyone who likes a good useful gadget that does lots of stuff we use frequently, and some cool stuff we would want to do.

Special UPDATE: I'm a very heavy set man, and while people have told me I snore, I didn't think much of it. Since I live alone, I really don't know much about what happens in my sleep. However, due to this watch I may want to get checked for Sleep Apnea, I took a nap and when I woke up I looked at my watch. My normal pulse is about 76-82 even at rest, and I noted my sleep average was in the low 50s, maybe thats normal I thought except, I noticed the lines in the pulse graph, some of them were missing! This either means the watch malfunctioned which it seems to be fine while I'm awake, it jumped from 52 most time while I'm asleep to 79 now. This with no gaps showing missing beats, since it takes readings only every so often that it displays as bars, it should be noted that my heart may have stopped for a minute or more in those instances where it missed. My dad had Sleep Apnea and though he died of Cancer, it in itself is a dangerous condition. When you don't get enough Oxygen, the body compensates by slowing the heart to conserve what it has, then it throttles up and down when it hits the danger zone. It's thought to create many cardiac events when sleeping. I take aspirin nightly, but it would be comforting to know if there is a treatable issue. At least I have something to tell my doctor now, which I really didn't feel anything was wrong before, just some tiredness and a little dry mouth on occasion. I'll update this if they find anything, if so this is worth it's weight in gold!
