review_title: REVERT EDIT:  The fitness gadget I've been waiting for
review_text:
EDIT: I have reverted my review to five stars after temporarily downgrading to four. I inferred some bad intent from a very minor and inconsequential flaw in Garmin's update process. The battery life of the device is 100% fine (and really amazingly great, when you come down to it) despite software updates. One merely has to do a power-down/power-up to reset the device and battery life returns to its normal excellent state.

============= original review below

I've been using HR monitors for over 20 years. I've used several Polar and Garmin, one Timex and two Fitbit devices. The vivoactive HR is the fitness gadget I've been waiting for my whole life.

PROS: I could go on for pages. It measures your HR with the little LED sensor on your wrist, but if you want to use it with a strap for extra accuracy, it will talk to the strap. Same for ANT+ bike speed/cadence sensors, foot pods, temperature sensors, all of which are really very reasonably priced. Best of all, it uploads information to phone/iPad/computer seamlessly and reliably.

This device is at about the price point of the Fitbit Surge. Well, I owned a Surge *and* a Blaze (deeply discounted through my employer), and they both just suck. If I were reviewing those devices, I could go on for pages about them, too. I won't spend a lot of keystrokes just slagging on Fitbit, but I will list a few things that I love about the Vivoactive HR as compared with those devices:

- The customizability of the watch faces is nearly infinite (see my closing comment below)
- Customizability of data displays *by activity type*
- The usability of the supporting apps on Android and IOS
- The watchband is not irritating to my skin (I don't have sensitive skin, but the Fitbits caused me real problems here)
- Readable in bright conditions without backlighting (see below negative comment about gestures)
- VERY reliable syncing with devices
- Buzzer "alarm" is attention-getting (to be fair, Fitbit was good about this, too)
- You can add/set alarms or timers directly from the watch, and easily
- Cool little list of customizable apps (lots of room for improvement here, but the framework is good)
- GPS sync is FAST; you even have a GLONASS option that you can customize by programmed activity
- The graphs and reports online are AMAZING - and if you don't like those, export the data to raw, TCX, GPX, Google Earth or CSV format and do whatever you like with it
- Battery life is astonishing; I charge it from 20% to 100% in about an hour and a half, and a full charge lasts 5-6 days (rather less if you use GPS heavily)

Support is FANTASTIC. When I first fired mine up, it installed a software update and froze up. I held the button down for 10 seconds with no effect. Thinking the update had bricked my new toy, I called the support line. A very pleasant, native-English-speaking young woman who was clearly NOT working from a stupid script written by idiot chimps answered the phone quickly and explained to me that I just didn't hold the button quite long enough. Holding it down for 15-20 seconds does an effective hard reset. The young lady was actually conversant with the features of the device and the software version in question. If every tech company did support like this, it would be a far better world.

CONS: I have some minor complaints here that might add up to docking the device a quarter-star or so if I could do that:

- Measurement of sleep just plain sucks, at least compared to Fitbit. This was the only thing Fitbit was really good at. With the Garmin, it *kind of* knows when I went to sleep and woke up, but in at least two cases now, I've gotten up to pee in the night and the Vivoactive has taken no notice. Garmin has a lot of work to do on this particular software feature.
- Wrist-flick "gesture" isn't very good at activating the backlight. Again, Fitbit was *excellent* at this. I have Casio and Oceanus watches that are *excellent* at this. The Vivoactive -- not so much. Again, maybe this can be fixed with coding.
- This thing looks a little clunky to be wearing as an everyday watch. Well, what do you want in such a full-featured device that packs its own GPS receiver? It's nowhere near as goofy-looking as the Fitbit Surge. It's a *little* bigger than the Blaze, but the Blaze doesn't have a GPS.
- There is an annoying bug in the feature where you can have it buzz if you stray above or below your target HR zone. Doesn't quite work exactly right.
- Garmin is seriously going to need to overhaul its "social media" feature on Garmin Connect. You can't control whether to post/share activities - either they post or they don't. Seriously, go troll the groups for people who post their runs and look at the map data that will literally lead you right to their doors. It's scary how stupid this is. And there are better and easier ways to give people control over their data. EDIT: they have added a robust and easy to use privacy setting.

But overall I am just tickled pink with this thing. And I'll leave you with a "pro tip": when you get it, go to the app on your phone (or whatever) and install the "SC8" watch face. You can thank me later. More importantly, you can thank the (Czech) author by sending him a couple of beers worth of money via Paypal. (I bought him two beers, because I like it twice as much as I expected to.)

review_text:
My rating is really about 3.5. I've had this device since May and have been wearing it continuously.

Pros:
-It fits! I have petite wrists and it fits with a couple of notches to spare.
-The HR monitor, though not incredibly sensitive, is very accurate. I have been to the cardiologist many times since May and every time they take my heart rate I check it against my wrist and it's within a couple of bpm of their reading.
-It has smart detection to pick up your activities if you forget to start the tracker (but see below).
-Water resistant makes it safe in the pool, ocean or shower.
-Does all the basic stuff an activity tracker should do (steps, sleep, etc).

Cons
-It's a little bulky. I stopped wearing it for sleep tracking because it was just too annoying.
-The smart activity tracker doesn't always work. It'll pick up a 15 minute walk during the workday but not know that I'm running on the treadmill at the gym for 40 minutes. Go figure.
-My biggest pet peeve, and what I feel is its biggest flaw: the distance tracking is off by at least .1 mile for every mile I run (outside AND at the gym), with or without GPS, apparently. Maybe it's just me? Maybe I don't swing my arms hard enough when I run? Idk, but it doesn't match the distance on MMR or on the treadmill.
-Subsequently, the pace is always off as well. The problem is that you can't manually edit your time / distance from the device OR the Garmin Connect site so tracking using the Garmin is completely useless. I end up using MapMyRun for live tracking and to manually log my treadmill runs.

review_text:
Let me start off by stating that I love this watch. I bought it as an upgrade to my forerunner 15 and since I am a data hog I love the extra information like how many flights of steps I have climbed. I use this watch as a weight loss/management tool, and it is great to track your steps, resting heart rate, etc.
I did some research and found that this watch is pretty accurate for calorie count, with one caveat: it has to stand alone. If you link it to My Fitness Pal (MFP) it way overinflates your available calories and here is why. The watch starts with a very low initial calorie count, and counts upward based on your steps and activity level. MFP starts with a base level of calories for an entire day based on your activity level, and you can add additional calories to your day by reporting workouts. Garmin reports these step calories as activity calorie adjustment, which is where the over-inflation comes in. I am posting pictures of relevant data... I have tried the link for negative calorie adjustment on MFP and it did not solve the problem. The only real way to resolve this issue is to disconnect Garmin Connect from MFP and manually report each exercise on MFP, or just delete the additional calorie adjustments in MFP.
Hope this helps...

review_title: Gave it a fair shot and am very happy! Super fast GPS and accurate activity tracking
review_text:
This is a feature-heavy fitness and activity tracker that deserves some time to get used to. The interface is relatively simple, but not aways straight-forward enough to be incredibly intuitive, making setup a little cumbersome. To be honest, when I first got mine, I was ready to return it. It didn't seem to be tracking my steps, and I couldn't get a run to start for some reason. But I gave it a chance and wore it for a day, and everything seemed to be working by day two, which was also around the time that the software update with the brightness fix was released. I've had it for two weeks, and I'm pretty happy with it now.

Pros:
- GPS connects very fast, usually within 5-10 seconds. My Nike usually took a couple minutes, even with a sync to pull current satellite locations.
- Charging is very fast. I think 0-100% would take about an hour.
- Battery life is good. I get about 5 days, which includes 2-3 runs and 2 bike rides, which all use GPS. And I'm probably only down to 20% at that point, not 0.
- Connecting my phone via Bluetooth was easy, and it's nice to see my phone's notifications while riding my bike. The connectivity seems strong--I get notifications from my phone even when I've left it upstairs and I'm downstairs.
- Calories (active and total) for the day is great.
- I like the "move" alerts, especially when I'm at work and need a reason to get away from my desk.
- Brightness was remedied quickly, and is now fine.
- The navigation feature seems very cool. I'm looking forward to trying it the next time I'm exploring on a run on vacation.

Needs improvement:
- BUG: sometimes when I flick through the widgets quickly I get repeats (i.e. I see weather twice before I see my steps for the day).
- TELLING TIME: I'd like the backlight to come on when I tap (or turn the watch towards me) so that I can see the watch face (and tell the time). Currently you have to swipe a little for the light, which often results in having to swipe back to the watch face. This makes it difficult to use it has a regular watch, since there's effort involved in being able to see the time. I'm using the Modern Analog face.
- Music controls don't work for Spotify. (I haven't tried iTunes.)
- I like being able to easily swap in different watch face designs, but do wish there was more to choose from.
- SETUP: All the different ways to connect, set up and adjust settings could be streamlined. Right now there are 3: the Garmin Express desktop app for watch settings and software updates; the Garmin Connect web app (for seeing fitness activity online); the Garmin Connect Mobile app (for syncing and seeing fitness activity with your phone). Plus you can also adjust some of the settings in the Settings area of the watch.
- It's bulky on a woman's wrist. It gets sweaty, so I always take it off after a run or if I'm basically done moving around for the day. I don't use it for sleep tracking. It's too bulky and I can't get used to wearing it to bed.

Running / biking (or any activity):
- The stats shown during an activity do not show the current time. This is a big deal for me. I run before I need to get ready for work, and I bike to work. Both of my main use cases put me in a situation where I want to know the time and need to swipe the screen while I'm all sweaty in order to see it.
- I'd like to be able to pause a run rather than wait for the auto-pause to kick in. (Maybe I'll get used to this, but there's quite a lag.)
- When ending a run it asks me two questions that I think are unnecessary, and I find annoying to answer when I'm sweaty and out of breath:
(1) "Save activity?" How about always save it and let me remove it from my data if I don't want it? I'm sure that the majority of tracked activities end up being saved.
(2) "Review details?" How about always show it for 15 seconds or so, and I can look at it if I want to? Nike got this one right.
Solution: When I end a run, show a summary for a few seconds, save it, and don't ask me anything.

review_title: Great Watch for Runners and Athletes
review_text:
There are so many disappointed buyers based on the reviews... I can understand why because of the way this watch is marked as an activity tracker for the general market. This is a watch designed for athletes who also want some "smart" features on their wrist. It is fantastic for that purpose and has a superb GPS that locks on in seconds, is completely waterproof, has an excellent and super-responsive touch-screen, and a built-in running app that rivals devices costing twice as much.

Personally, I was looking for a watch/tracker for running. Anything else the device offered would be frosting on the cake. I went so far as to go to a Garmin tech session at the local running store. They Garmin rep told me that the difference between the Vivoactive (HR and non HR) was the data fields that were available to be displayed on the data screens during an activity. There are other differences, of course, but unless you care about VO2 max or other a couple other features that are only available on the Forerunners, this is a real bargain in a running watch. Plus, on top of running, it can also track rowing, cycling, swimming, walking and quite a few other activities which most of the other Forerunners cannot. If you do activities other than running, and want something for $250, this is the watch for you.

I see a lot of comments on the screen in other reviews. The screen is dull indoors but is readable with the backlight. IMO, this device was made to be used outdoors. Outdoors in sunlight (or on a cloudy day), this watch is amazing. I can't believe how crisp and bright it is outside. The best part (to me) is that the screen never turns off. The way I use the watch, I have to charge it about every 3 days, but that is 2 more days than I could go between charging my Apple Watch. The mid May update added a brighter backlight option. While this doesn't turn the screen into anything resembling any of the Android or Apple smart watches out there, it does make the screen bright enough to read and use indoors.

I used the Apple Watch for a few months before getting the Vivoactive HR... The Apple Watch is a fantastic device with a lot of potential, but it is designed for the masses and not athletes. I downloaded a few of the running apps and even signed up for a year with one of them. The applications are great, but the Apple Watch doesn't have the horse-power to keep up. On a run, I would have to lower my arm to my side and then bring it up to get the screen to come on so I could look at my time/pace -- 1/2 the time it would not come on so I would have to lower my arm and try again -- sometimes a few times. Very frustrating. The heart rate on the Apple watch was useless... The Garmin watch is always on so just look down and my current pace, heart rate and distance are shown. SO much better! The Vivoactive HR is designed to be an athlete's watch. It does not try to do everything, but what it does, it does quickly and well.

The GPS is incredible. When I put the watch into a mode (walk/run) it locks on the the GPS in seconds. I've never waited for the watch to find a GPS signal... ever... I think I spend more time putting my dog on her leash.

There are a couple cons that I see with this watch. One can probably be fixed with software but the other is hardware related. The device is horrible at tracking my sleep. It usually overestimates my sleep by at least an hour -- I typically go to bed at 9:30 and read for a half-hour -- the Vivoactive HR sometimes has me sleeping at 8:30. I'm not sure what algorithm they use, but it doesn't work for my sleep pattern at all. Luckily, I know how much sleep I get and don't care to track it. Secondly, the marketing tells you that other apps and data fields can be added to the device. Yes, they can, but only a few. Once you get a few 3rd party apps/data fields/widgets into the watch, it runs out of memory. So, while it is possible to add 3rd party apps, you have to be very selective on which ones you want to add.

Lastly, let me get into their iPhone software and website. I feel the iPhone software is excellent. It is fun to use and shows me summary information screens that are fun to read and informative. You tap on the summary information and dig into the details including heart rate, pace, cadence and other useful information. I won't call the software intuitive, but once you learn how it works, you'll quickly be able to find any information you need. The website is a little cluttered and confusing. I appreciate that there is so much information available -- I feel a lot of devices and manufacturers try to dumb down information for the masses. I appreciate having it all available.

With heavier usage obviously that drops, likewise when I was absolutely slammed at work with no time for outside walking or running, I got nearly 2 weeks on one charge!

I do have one major issue and why I took a star off, the stair counts are terrible. Very random how many stairs it will miss in a day. Once is ran 8 floors in my building and only 1 counted. Usually though it counts 1 out of every 3 floors. As a stair counter it's worthless. Step counting, rowing, and running are pretty accurate.

The heart rate sensor is excellent. I've watched it side by side with my treadmill and I checked my pulse manually, each time it matched within a beat.

review_text:
Revised review (1 star) while the watch seemed to track heart rate accurately initially (and still does if I'm just walking) I have had major issues with the heart rate tracking during mixed cardio activities. The BPM figures seemed excessively high compared to actual, which I validated by intermittent manual heart rate checks. I also did several mixed cardio workouts wearing the Vivoactive on one wrist and my Forerunner45s on the other, and saw differences of as much as 50BPM between the data on the two watches, with the Vivoactive measuring high. I contacted Garmin support and after multiple submissions of data, they picked two samples (1 walking, 1 cardio) out of many and said that the results were within reason. Never mind that there were many others that were not within reason! I cannot use this watch to track my cardio activity, Garmin says there's nothing wrong with it, and I'm stuck. Do not buy this product. In fact, I don't recommend buying ANY Garmin product - their warranty and support are useless.

Original review (3 star) This watch replaced my Forerunner 45s, which I liked until the sockets that held the band broke and could not be fixed. I selected the Vivoactive 4s because it was closest in size to my previous small watch, and had all the features of the old watch plus additional features of interest. The 4s seems to be accurate in tracking steps, distance, time, and heart rate. Cosmetically, the watch I received has a light gold case but silver buckle on its dusty pink band, which doesn't look great but is probably not noticeable to others. The watch faces included by Garmin have sparse feature content, and I do not like the fake analog hands; however, I was able to download a very good digital watch face free from Garmin Connect.

The major drawback of this watch is the miserable performance on counting stair climbs and descents. The results are extremely inconsistent - sometimes high, sometimes low. I have read Garmin's suggestions on correcting this, which tell you to swing your arms while going up and down (maybe outdoors if you're on a hill, but what kind if nutcase swings their arms going up and down stairs?) If this is Garmin's solution for excluding altitude changes such as riding in an elevator, surely there is a better method. I am resigned to accepting the lousy performance of this feature and just not tracking stair climbing, but I could have purchased a cheaper watch without the stairs climbed feature.

review_title: Battery failure at just under two years.
review_text:
The functionality of this watch is great. It tracks and trends a lot of data, and the app presents several options for reviewing your data. I've used it for running, cycling, hiking and several other activities over the last 22 months. Unfortunately, the battery spontaneously failed on me the other day. It, literally, went from holding a charge for three or four days, to not being able to hold charge for a single day.

It's pricey purchase to have to consider repeating every couple years. I read several reviews about other customers having battery failures before I even bought the watch. Some experienced it within the first few months, others within a year or two of ownership. I had hoped that the chances of such a failure were slim, and I took a chance on the watch and the brand.

Do not purchase the Garmin Vivoactive 4 if GPS tracking for runs or Bluetooth connectivity are important to you. After 5 months of use I am ready to dump this watch. I changed my initial rating from 3 starts to 2 stars. Bluetooth is horrible. GPS accuracy is very bad. Constantly records shorter distances then actually traveled. If the Vivoactive4 lost .25 miles in 8 to 10 mile run then I would consider that acceptable. Check out the complaints on the Garmin forums. There are a large number of complaints about the Bluetooth and GPS. My guess is the placement of the sensors in the watch is the issue because the many updates to the software / GPS/Bluetooth just do not fix the issue.

I previously owned the first version of the Vivoactive 3 ( non music) There is lots to like about the Vivoactive 4 including the looks. The biggest issue I have, and the reason I gave it 3 stars, is the Bluetooth. It is bad. Not nearly as reliable as the Vivoactive 3. It regularly disconnects after walking 15 feet away. It will also sometimes disconnect from my phone when the phone is an inch or two away from the watch. GPS was initially bad but the last GPS update fixed the issues. Just hoping the Bluetooth software gets fixed soon. I have a Samsung Galaxy S10+. Yes I am up to date on all the software, apps, and watch software. Not sure why there is a huge difference in Bluetooth connectivity between the Vivoactive 3 and the 4.

I broke down and got a new biking computer and the watch can broadcast my heartrate to the computer so it's still useful. review_title: Heart Rate is Horribly Inaccurate, Customer Service is Terrible
review_text:
I have been contemplating an upgrade from my Fitbit Charge for a while now, and thought this Garmin Vivoactive 4s would fit the bill for my smaller-than-average wrist. When it became a black Friday deal, I took the plunge. I loved all the additional features I was getting in an upgraded SmartWatch and the additional tracking features that this model had over equivalent Fitbit models. I did think that using it was not as intuitive to use as the Fitbit, and the app was overly complicated, but that was something I could get used to.

My main complaint about this watch and why I ended up returning it and going back to my old Fitbit is that it did not give me accurate heartrate readings at all during exercise. Not that Fitbit was dead-on accurate either, but it was close enough. This Garmin gave me readings that were 50-100% higher than my actual manually-taken pulse rate. This is completely unacceptable. The heartrate readings were OK at rest and seemed to be OK when recording a yoga workout, but were totally off on the cardio setting. I did four very mild cardio workouts (equivalent of brisk walking) using the watch where I know for a fact that my HR never went above 120-130 (because I took my pulse manually). Meanwhile, the watch was giving me readings of 160-190, and reporting average heart rates of 140-150! At one point, I took my pulse and I counted a BPM of 98, and the watch told me I was at 192.

When I contacted Garmin customer support via chat about this, among other things, I was directed to a Garmin webpage (which I had already read) about heart rate accuracy and told that the watch only supports certain types of activity, HIIT not being one of them. This is completely ridiculous for a number of reasons. Firstly, I was very clear that I was getting these wild readings on only very mild cardio workouts. I did mention that my heart rate doesn't even get that high during HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training) workouts, and for some reason the CS rep went out of their way to tell me that HIIT cardio is not supported. Were they even paying attention to what I said? Secondly, HIIT, Tabata, and other interval training is a common training mode for people into fitness. How can you not support these training modes if you are selling a fitness watch? Overall, support was horrible. They even said that they don't bother to troubleshoot newly purchased watches - they only do return/replace. I indicated that I only wanted a replacement if they thought that the issue was a defect in the watch, but not if the watch by design doesn't support cardio activities that I normally do. They couldn't tell me if they thought it was only that one watch that was defective or if I would have problems in general due to the design of the watch. For this reason, I decided to just return it and go back to Fitbit. I don't have the time or patience to have to test out another replacement. As much as I love the other aspects about this watch, I bought it primarily as a fitness tracker. If it can't even get ballpark heart rates when I am working out, that is a complete dealbreaker. Heart rate is the one thing you need to get at least somewhat right if you want to get a good gauge of your workouts.

review_title: High expectations; not half the product that One was
review_text:
I had a Fitbit One for several months and loved it. It tracked steps accurately, counted elevation gain (a cool trick for runners/cyclists) and did a reasonably good job of monitoring sleep. The cons were that I had to clip it to my bra (most women's pants/skirts are pocketless), and remembering to stick it in that funny little wristband for sleep monitoring. But I was a huge fan of the Fitbit platform, and excitedly waited in line for the backordered Flex. After all, a wristband format would solve the issues that I had with the clip.

The first thing I noticed was that the Flex no longer monitors elevation change. This was disappointing because I liked to see the relative change after a run or ride. The second thing I noticed is that the step count is inaccurate. A 1.5-mile walk to and from my son's school was tracked consistently and accurately with the One. With the Flex, I would get credit for about 60% of the steps. On a trip to Europe, I walked high and low through a lovely hilly town. MapMyRun said that I had walked 6+ miles. Flex logged it at roughly 3.5 miles.

I know other Flex users who tested the devices together, wearing both the One and Flex for a period to see how closely they aligned. One estimated a routine 30-40% undercount in the Flex. (Again, basing step count vs. mapped miles walked.)

To activate sleep tracking, you have to tap the device. And tap it. And tap it repeatedly. Eventually it will enter sleep mode. What makes it enter sleep mode consistently? Riding over bumpy spots in the road, tapping a wooden spoon on the edge of the pot, or clapping my hands. So if I don't keep track of it, the Flex thinks that I'm randomly falling asleep throughout the day.

Last week, I charged the battery overnight. It tracked hundreds of steps that I "walked" throughout the night while the device was plugged into the computer; I have no idea what it thought I was doing all night. When I put it back on in the morning, it tracked nothing -- literally zero steps -- for the first two and a half hours of wear.

The battery ran out last night, and I decided this morning that I won't bother recharging it. Why am I wearing something that doesn't give an accurate count?

The two stars are for the improvement in the form factor over the clip of the One. Other than that, it's pretty much useless.

review_text:
I've been wearing this since August 21st of 2013. With that being said, I think enough time has passed to make a proper assessment of the product.

I like it! I read a few articles here and there about various wrist trackers before I bought this one, and I'm pretty satisfied with my purchase. Lets get the pros/cons out of the way:

Pros:

- Battery lasts *longer* than Fitbit advertises. They advertise 5 days, but I easily get a week to a week and a half, depending on activity.
- Hardly notice it on my wrist, wears in the shower just fine.
- Monitors pretty much everything I want, and the website works great
- They made awesome updates to the mobile app recently

Cons:

- Limited smartphone sync support (more on this later)
- The wristband design *can* lend to foul smells (more on this later as well)

The pros definitely outweigh the cons, though. I was slightly disappointed (and admittedly, stupid about this) in finding out that Bluetooth 4.0 is not backwards compatible, which means I couldn't sync with my smartphone. The fact that it could wirelessly sync (while the Jawbone Up couldn't) really appealed to me. However, the package comes with a Bluetooth 4.0 dongle that works very well with OS X and Windows (no Linux unfortunately :( ). I've relegated my Mac to a Fitbit sync machine, and it works perfectly. I wanted to sync as much as possible, but I've come to realize that you really don't need to. You just go about your day, then sync whenever you happen to get within 20 feet of your computer. It's all automatic, and uploads the results immediately to fitbit.com (along with the mobile app).

As for everyone talking about the smell, this definitely seems true. However, what I do is just remove the fitbit from the wristband once a day, blow out any moisture, and put it back. It's a 30 second process, and as a result, I've never had a funky smell from my fitbit. I highly recommend doing this, and it's not much of a hassle, so....

All in all, I'm very satisfied. I only took a star away because of the small smartphone support.

UPDATE 12/27/13:

I recently got a new phone (the Moto X; fantastic phone by the way!), and Fitbit happened to add support for smartphone syncing. I'm even happier than I was before, so I added another star :). The app is really neat as well, as you can track your steps live. It's a little bit buggy sometimes with syncing, but it will always sync on the second try, then remain connected. It's honestly not even a bother, so meh.

I plan on using this tracker until it just completely dies, then upgrade to the Force :)

UPDATE 5/3/14:

I've reduced my review from 5 to 3 stars, and this is for the fact that I have been through two wristbands already. The slot where you put the Flex becomes cracked if you do my daily habit of removing the Flex to clear out the moisture inside. This is a tremendous design flaw in itself; I shouldn't have to worry about the wristband cracking, especially since I want to remove gross bacteria from the inside. If this continues, I might just have to switch over to the Jawbone UP24, because this is getting ridiculous.

UPDATE 3/14/15:

I completely stopped using my Flex. Reason being is that it completely died after only a year of usage. Fitbit replaced it, however, having the unit completely die on me left a bad taste in my mouth. I'm not sure I can really recommend this product anymore

review_title: HR monitor on mine is 35 beats (per min!) faster than actual HR and other HR watches
review_text:
Unfortunately the heart rate monitor on mine is consistently 30-35 beats (per min!) faster than other similar fitness/running watches. Considering an average resting HR is 60-100 BPM (and less for athletes), it's extreme to have it be 30-35 beats higher, which in some instances can make it double what it really is.

We also have a Garmin Vivosmart HR, Fitbit Blaze, and a Fenix 3 (with HRM-run heart rate strap), so we have 3 others we compared it with. Then of course, manually taking HR the old fashioned way.

While sitting:
Fitbit Blaze - 76
Vivosmart HR - 73
Manually taking HR - 74
Garmin Forerunner 35 - 101

I noticed the issue the first day I wore it. I was sitting, and glanced down and it said my HR was 140! Yikes. I immediately took my HR manually, and it was 100. The watch continued to keep taking my HR (the numbers switching on the screen, so I know it was actively taking it) - they were going from 140, to 139, 141, 138, etc.

We purchased this for our son, a high school track athlete. The date on the display is wrong and can't be reset on the device as the device receives the date from a satellite. The Garmin website said, "We’ve identified an issue with this product that causes the date to be wrong after the GPS Rollover on April 6th, 2019. However, all functions not dependent on date and/or time will continue to work normally. Due to the age of the device we have determined we will not fix this issue.

What does that mean for my Garmin?

o The date determined by the GPS will be wrong

o Position, velocity, navigation, and all other functionality not dependent on date and/or time will continue to work normally

What is GPS Week Rollover?

The GPS satellite system communicates the date via a week number that is limited to 1024 weeks (about 20 years). On April 6th, 2019 the week numbers broadcast by the satellites will “rollover” to zero. If GPS receivers don’t account for this rollover in their software, it will calculate the wrong date and/or time.

review_title: I can't even describe my disappointment with this watch
review_text:
I can't even describe my disappointment with this watch. I read all the reviews and I had hope that the Garmin had improved since 2012 when I got my last watch from them, that the satellite syncing wouldn't take so long like it used to. Everyone I know who has a Garmin said that it's super fast. I must have got a lemon because mine takes anywhere between 3 to 5 minutes to sync. I contacted Garmin, who I had been told have excellent customer service, and their recommendation was to sync my watch with my phone every day. I tried that. It did help a little, but I shouldn't have to do that to get it to sync to satellites. I also shouldn't have to do that every day! I live on a small island, it's not like I'm moving very far from the last location I ran from each time I use this. I don't understand why the satellite syncing feature would have to be updated on a daily basis with my phone. I was not impressed with the advice and the blase and uncaring from the person I spoke to.

It also takes a long time to sync to my phone (Garmin agreed that this is unusual), as it can take up to 5 minutes. Which is annoying, I have better things to do with my time than babysit my watch syncing.

I can walk around my bedroom for a few minutes and it doesn't notice I'm walking so even counting steps isn't so accurate. I've been walking down the street looking at the step counter and seeing it not register my movement.

Overall a huge disappointment. When it works, it's great, but honestly, Map My Fitness on my phone is quicker and easier. I can turn it on and within 10 seconds I can go. If I was trying to use this watch for a race, I'd miss the start because I'd be waiting for it to sync. Or it might start in time. It's so hit and miss it's hard to tell.

One positive is that it does have a pretty band and I think the heart rate monitor is accurate but I don't know for sure as I've nothing to test it against. Another positive is that the interval timer on it is pretty good and very useful.

Distances I'm not sure who's being inaccurate but my phone and my watch get different distances even though one is in my right hand and the other on my left wrist. I'm told that that can be fixed with doing something in the settings but I haven't bothered trying as I've ceased using this for anything but a step counter (even if it is inaccurate).

I hate leaving negative reviews but I can't even begin to describe how disappointed I am with this watch and Garmins response to my complaint (I only contacted them the once as the person I spoke to was useless). Everyone else I know who has one (different models) find these watches amazing but this will be the last Garmin I buy unfortunately. Which is a shame.

review_text:

I've had the replacement for less than 4 weeks, and with this one, it sporadically stops recording data. A long chat session with Garmin support revealed that 1) There is a latency delay with their servers but some of the data will probably show up eventually, and 2) The watch stopped recording at 4am and they don't know why. According to them, it shouldn't happen again. I'm not convinced.

I don't need all the bells and whistles that come with this watch. The pacing function is pretty useless with limited configurability. But I paid a premium to get a good GPS watch that syncs with MapMyRun and MyFitnessPal so that I can track my various routes and maintain data over time. For that, it works well WHEN it works.

But now I'm stuck with a watch that only works when it feels like it.

==========ORIGINAL REVIEW===========
I like it just fine.... but it stopped working after 5 weeks (just past the 30-day return window). Problem: could no longer connect to charge. Connection wasn't connecting. After long chat and troubleshooting with support, they offered to exchange it for a working model....

Other quibbles: Steps are way way off. I calibrated my steps and double checked several times, but before I even get out of bed in the morning it will say I've done over 1000 steps....which suggests it's not the step calibration that's off, but something wrong with the device itself. Also, it only integrates with myfitnesspal, which sucks if you have an extensive record on some other platform (and have prepaid a year's membership).

Although Garmin is replacing the device, the experience has been so poor that I would prefer to have gotten a refund so that I could buy another brand of watch.

review_title: If you are latex sensitive, this is not your watch
review_text:
The information may be hidden somewhere in the product materials but I didn't see it before buying. The watch band has latex in it. That became very apparent after I started wearing it for extended periods. I had to glue some cloth strips on the underside to be able to wear it. It also turns out the chest band HR monitor also has latex in it.

The wrist sensor for pulse rate is a random number generator unless you crank it down to the point it's uncomfortable. Even then, it has random changes in HR that have nothing to do with activity. If you want accurate HR, you need the chest band sensor. However the unit uses the wrist pulse by default, so if you are not recording an activity, you have at best an approximate.

The unit is surprising good on tracking indoor treadmill distance for me, it's usually within 0.02 for a 3 mile run.

The elevation changes are much closer to actual numbers than my previous units.

The choice of activities to record is limited so I'm often going back after synchronization and changing the category. However, it does have the common ones and it's easy to switch.

Overall, I wound not buy it again because of the latex problem. If that's not your issue, it's a good unit at reasonable cost.

review_text:
If you want a device that gives you accurate time of day and date, this is it. If you want something to help with your efforts to train or keep fit, this is only marginally functional. My main interest in a GPS watch is to tell me how far I have run or cycled and give me some basic information about those workouts. In that respect, this has been a waste of money.

In the past, I have had a Garmin 210, 610, and 910. I lost the 210. The 610 was the best one I had except the band kept falling off at the hinges and a few times the screen went completely black in the middle of a run. I still have the 610 and it works but I had a 910 which was pretty reliable until it completely died in the middle of a run about two months ago. Could not be revived so I resorted back to my old 610 with super-glued watch band while I researched another device. They all have mixed reviews so I settled on the Forerunner 35. Mistake.

Measuring Distance. It is all over the place. I have tested it against my 610, several apps and marked courses like paths that are known to be accurately measured. Some days it is ahead by as much as .10 miles, some days behind, some days right on. Some days, it starts behind and "catches" up (how does that happen), other days the opposite. And no I am not running or biking in tunnels or underpasses where it will lose satellite connections. It just varies a a lot.

Pace. I have two wearable device and set two apps and Forerunner 35 always gives me a different MPH during the activity. Even while the two devices are giving me the same elapsed time, the pace is different.

Heart Rate. Way off. That does not surprise me since I think it is just about impossible to get an accurate heart rate from a device worn on the outside of my wrist. I get a higher heart rate when I take a pulse when I stop at a traffic light during a run even if it takes me about 20 seconds to start counting.

Calories Burned. Way off. My typical week day morning bike ride is between 25 and 26 miles. It tells me I burn about 200 calories. Even apps that isn't measuring heart rate will give me about 700 calories for that distance.

Step Count. Completely useless. This morning, I ran 6.1 miles by its measure. That is accurate base on other sources; the Forerunner 35 told me I had taken 0 steps. This happens regularly. Fitbit gives me about 10,000 steps for that distance. When I bike 25 miles, it gives me about 250 steps.
Fitbit gives me about 10,000 steps here too. I don't count steps as part of my training but we have frequent step count competitions at work and I participate in those. In fact, my employer gives each interested employee a free fitness tracker.

The bottom line is I am looking for a new device in which I can have some confidence. This one isn't it. Sadly, all the Forerunners seem to have the same issues.

GARMIN, PLEASE BRING BACK THE 610.

Update. August 16, 2018. I have had this watch only six months. Now it takes quite a bit of time to connect to satellites. The worse part is now it has problems with my bike rides. Two days ago, I rode for 25+ miles for about 1 hour 45 minutes and it recorded .58 miles at a pace of 2.3 miles/hour. Today, I rode for 23.2 miles and it recorded 17.53 miles. I use Strava app as well and I know the general distance of the courses I ride so I know this thing is completely malfunctioning. What a waste of money.

review_text:
The Garmin forerunner 35 is a basic gps for tracking workouts, but it is not very accurate and is very limited in what it can do.

Good:
-Light weight
-Easy to follow menus
-Once it finds gps it stays connected

Bad:
-Takes forever to find gps signal. Make sure you start it way before you want to start a workout. It often goes into sleep mode because it takes so long.
-It is very inaccurate in tracking distance. I tested the 35 against two other higher end Garmins and the 35 was off by 1.3 miles after tracking for 19 miles.
-You can't track elevation gain on the watch. You can see it on the app. To me this is really dumb. All I care about is total distance, total time and total elevation gain. That's all I want to see and know. Why this can't be on the watch baffles me.
-The elevation that the watch calculates after syncing with the app is way off.
-The app is super intrusive and is always running in the background even if the watch is off. All I want to do is sync my workouts so I can see all the details. I ended up installing it on a tablet I rarely use because I didn't want the app on my phone.
-The watch takes forever to sync with the app. Sometimes it just gives up. Super annoying.

review_title: DO NOT WASTE YOUR MONEY - Horrible tracking in ALL METRICS

It regularly stops displaying a pace altogether. I expect some variables but most of the time I can’t tell my pace at all. I may as well run without a watch. The first time I swam with this thing it short circuited. I wasn’t deep sea diving, just swimming in a regular pool. I got a replacement because it was still in warranty. However the heart rate tracking on both have been pbeyond horrible. I run, row, bike, swim and compete in CrossFit. More often than not the watch registers my HR in the mid 80’s regardless of intensity. I’ve had this register my heart rate as low 33 BEATS PER MINUTE during a workout. I can be sitting on my couch watching Netflix and my heart rate will register as 125. I don’t expect it to be as accurate as a chest strap but for real, 33 BPM!? I had a Garmin 235 that was far more accurate in tracking my runs. Not even the step tracking on this watch is accurate. Get a Whoop if you’re serious about any sort of fitness tracking. This thing was a complete waste of money. It’s been such a headache I’m never buying a garmin again.

review_text:
This is my first Amazfit product, so I cannot really comment on how well it works in comparison to other watches by the same manufacturer. But - it is affordable, looks very good, and works well out of the box. I was in need of a smart watch with a GPS tracker that would work with or without a mobile phone. This model checks all these boxes: the GPS works without a mobile phone nearby and seems very accurate. After completing a walking route that I know very well (and know the distance too), the GPS tracker measured my speed, distance walked, and mapped the walk very accurately (giving me the same numbers that I get by using my mobile phone GPS with apps like MapMyWalk or Strava). Its heart rate monitor is accurate too, but its oxygen (SpO2) meter seems to be inaccurate (I believe other reviewers also mentioned this).

Other observations: system updates are very quick (take about 2-3 minutes only). The Zepp app is reasonably easy to use and quite intuitive - one needs to go to "Profile" and then to "My Devices" (or "Add a Device") to add the watch and sync it with the app. Battery life appears to be quite good and the watch will keep charge for days. Charging is quick and takes about 1.5 to 2 hours (from the battery being down to 20% or below). The image is bright with vivid colors (becomes somewhat dim if the sun is strong) and the touch screen is responsive. The watch is very easy to use and there are plenty of options to cover many outdoor activities.

Overall - the Bit U Pro is among the most affordable GPS-enabled smart watches out there and, more importantly, it is well-made and offers lots of value.

review_title: GREAT substitute for more expensive fitness trackers
review_text: I had used a Garmin Vivo fit II for years as my fitness tracker. It was a basic step counter that interfaced with my employers health monitoring. As a Registered Respiratory Therapist I wanted a fitness monitor that would do more. I was reluctant to spend big bucks for some of the fancier ones. So, I started looking at the Amazfit models. The one negative I can say is for step tracking it is slightly on the light side. I feel my Garmin device was more accurate. With the Amazfit you have to be swinging your arm to get a accurate count. The Amazfit does a good job on sleep tracking with slot of info in the app. The cardiac monitoring is very good and accurate. If you are looking for an actual cardiac tracing you will have to spend more. It does show if you are in warm up, fat buring, aerobic or anaerobic zone based on heart rate. The pulse odometer feature is surprisingly accurate. I have compared it with multiple hospital grade units and have been very satisfied. It took awhile to get the Alexa feature to even turn on and it still does not do much and I am not sure why? The app has a great deal of additional info. Battery life has been acceptable, I average about 7 to 9 days between charges. It takes about two hours to charge when down to10% or less. I have to give this watch a strong buy recommendation, for the price I do not feel it can be beat. The only other issues are the instructions that are included are not great and the manufacturer has not been responsive to questions I have sent them. But again, cannot beat the price.

review_title: Great device thus far...won't go back to FitBit...some issues
review_text:
I was sick of paying the high Fitbit prices only to have the device die within a year. I saw this device and thought it was reasonably priced and had the same core features I had with Fitbit. I really only use the step tracking, time, and sleep tracking, as well as heartbeat and weather. I'm really not seeing a major difference...in fact...I think the device interface and app are better than Fitbit.

The issues I have found:
*There do not seem to be a ton of 12hr watch face options. There are still a bunch, but not as large of a library as the 24hr ones.
*Even with a 12hr watch face and my device set to display in 12hr format, when charging, the device displays the time in 24hr format.
*Even with a 12hr watch face and my device set to display in 12hr format, when using the weather app, the sunset time is displayed in 24hr format.
*The sleep tracker trackers both your bedtime sleep and naps (which is great) to total up your total sleep time. However, the app is the only place that provides the total sleep time. The watch itself will only display the first sleep session. If you go to bed and sleep for 6hr, wake up, and take a 2hr nap in the afternoon, the watch will say you only slept for 6hrs but the app will say you slept for 8.
*I haven't tried to drain the watch battery completely to see how long it takes, but based on the battery percentage icon, I don't see how it could possibly last 9 days.

All in all...still a great watch...and I've been very happy with it. Won't be going back to Fitbit.

review_title: An improvement over BIP. Great value!
review_text:
I was looking for an upgrade to my Amazfit Bip that has been a good watch for the past couple years. As an Android user, the Apple Watch isn't an option. I value battery life and notifications as high priority features with the other features being nice, but not essential. I'm on day three with the Bip U Pro and it's exceeded expectations! It seems to drop about 10-15% of battery life per day which would be in line for a 9 day battery life. The screen is bright and detailed! It's just a little bit thicker than the Bip but still not too big. Pretty light and I really don't notice I'm wearing it. The screen isn't always on like the Bip but it usually lights up when I raise my wrist to look at it.

I like the added features of music control and Alexa integration the U Pro comes with. I haven't seen any reviews that include the Alexa integration actually working, so it was a bit of a roll of the dice on if it would be worth it. It is! It requires a click to activate rather than being wake word activated like my Echo, but that's probably for the best. It accepts the request via voice once it's listening. Then it responds via text on the watch face. It's good for basic questions with "what I found on the web" type responses. Weather forecasts has some icons with it. I'm sure there is more it can do that I'll find, but overall neat to play with.

I've updated the watch face, would be neat to be able to develop my own. The SpO2 measurement seems pretty hit and miss. I guess I wouldn't use it to decide if I need oxygen flying or climbing or something. Out of four attempts, it only was able to find a reading once. The heartrate seems to be more reliable.

For a $70 watch, it's great!

review_text:
When i review items, i like to give first impressions of the item and then give it about 2 weeks to come up with my results on how i feel about it.

First impressions:

Packaging: 10/10 Looks sleek and very well put together. Not too much paperwork and guides are straight forward

Product: I love that the headphones charge in the case and that the case isn't too big or too small. I like that there were different ear clips sizes and different ear bud sizes. Sound output is awesome when connecting to my S7 Edge. I like that is has the option to let in outside noise so you are aware of the noise thats happening around you. I love love love the you can connect it to any device that has bluetooth so its not only for one specific brand.I love that the charging pod holds a charge so it doesn't have to always be connected to an outlet when charging; perfect when on the go! One of the best things is the look of them, they just look amaze!

The negatives: I have 2 phones, the S7 Edge and my iPhone 7plus and multiple tablets. Works seamlessly with my Edge but anything else connecting via bluetooth is a miss 99% of the time. The audio comes out distorted and sounds horrible. You get better sound from headphone at your local dollar store. I also dislike the fit of the headphones. There are different bud sizes and different ear clips, but its a hassle to fit them onto your ears. I find myself shoving them inside my ear to keep them in place. That negative leads into the negative with them being touch sensitive. When putting them in your ear you find yourself pressing against the touch sensors and either changing songs or making selections you didn't want to happen like starting a workout. One of the biggest negatives is that the battery on the headphones only hold about an hour to and hour and a half. Thats not enough to use on a road trip or even on normal use throughout the day.

Final thoughts: After about a month of use with these headphones/Buds, I like to idea and the concept of them but i think they missed majorly on execution. I think to myself that if they rushed production to be ahead of apple and not focusing on the overall product...Note 7....Hmmmmm. There are too many issues with these buds for me and i don't think i would recommend them to family for purchase. Purchase price at $150-$200 seems too steep for a product with this many issues and not that great functionality....

Good try Samsung, ill be waiting for your improved version in the near future.

review_title: I really wanted to like these
review_text:
This is a brilliant product in theory. I really wanted to like these headphones. But for me they have two major downfalls. The sound quality is good, but not quite loud enough and certainly not bass driven enough for a music lover like myself. My second issue is the battery life. These have to be charged every day. If the case was actually capable of giving five full charges as advertised, this wouldn't have been as much of an issue. But even if you don't use the headphones after charging them up, they and the charging carrying case will be drained of battery life by the next day.

They handle taking phone calls surprisingly well. You can hear the caller with good clarity and the caller on the other end can hear everything on your end just fine.

They fit snugly in the ear and don't fall out under normal circumstances.

Touch controls work well, but knowing where exactly to touch is an issue.

I said I had two major issues with these, we'll I forgot about another annoying thing. The gear app that you use as a companion to these headphones is indicating to me that a software update is available for them and that to access the update I need to put them in their case and connect to a computer. Well I don't have a desktop or laptop computer. I do all my computing on my android phone, my iPad Air and my Xbox One. So who knows what I'm missing out on by not upgrading the software. It's too bad that software updates couldn't have been downloaded to my phone and then somehow ported over to the headphones.

If you are willing to look past getting about an hour of use (duration of a workout perhaps) between charges, having to charge them every night, getting less than ideal volume and bass levels and the 200 dollar price tag then these may be right for you. For me, I have a bit of buyers remorse and wish I'd returned them while I still could. I think as a first generation product, there's lots of room to grow. Hopefully the Gear Icon X2 (or whatever they call the next iteration) will be much better.

review_title: These are awful.  AVOID.  Not worth anywhere near $200
review_text:
Unfortunately, these are not good enough to cost any more than 20 bucks. I received these as a gift from my wife to make it easier to listen to music while walking my dogs. My phone is a Samsung Galaxy S6 Edge. I'll try to describe what I like and what I really don't like.

Fit: 3/5. They are somewhat large, but stay in place. They must have lots of tech packed into them, so it's understandable that these are a bit larger than wired earbuds would be. However, they start to get uncomfortable after about 30 min. They also come loose occasionally, so I constantly keep pressing them back in. It's hard to imagine they would fit comfortably for someone with small ears.

Sound: 2/5. The sound itself is actually not terrible. However, they skip. A LOT. I can rarely make it through a song without skipping all over the place. I haven't dealt with skipping during my music since I used to listen to CDs on crappy CD players. It makes me feel like we're going back in time. Watch, soon Samsung will come out with music on cassette tape. Maybe Samsung expects me to rewind Spotify when I'm done listening...

Controls: 2/5. These are controlled by touch, which in theory is an awesome feature. One touch pauses/resumes your music. Two will skip a song. Double-touch and hold to get to the menu for "Start Workout" and "Enable Ambient Sound." Three taps will go back a song. Two taps will answer a call. Also, notifications come through to let you know what app beeped (e.g. you'll hear a notification and then "GMAIL" played through the headset. Pretty cool. Unfortunately, sometimes these don't register my touch. Other times they are too sensitive. It always seems to be that when I can tell someone is trying to talk to me, I can't pause the music; it just wont accept touch. This is particularly problematic because they are so small, people have no idea I'm wearing headphones and because I have dogs, people just assume I want to talk to them. So I have no idea what they are saying while I try to first fumble to get the music to stop by playing in my ears, then fumble to get my phone out and stop it there. The whole thing takes 10-20 seconds until I get frustrated and just pull em out of my ears and jam them in a pocket. Which makes me uneasy, cause they cost 200 freaking bucks and I don't want them to break or fall out and get lost.

Call Quality: 2/5. For some reason, phone calls only play through the right ear phone, not both. My wired Samsung earbuds play really, really high quality sound during phone calls. These, for some reason, do not. There's no HD sound on these, or it doesn't sound like there is. Also, they skip sometimes during calls as well. If you try to take them out of your ears and shove em in a pocket, and then put your phone on speaker, the phone keeps trying to pair with the headphones and automatically goes back to bluetooth. It makes calls impossible. However, people who are on the other end of the line say my voice comes through really clearly.

General Quality: 1/5. This is the part that really makes me mad, and what prompted me to come write a review. The quality of these is garbage. They come in a charge case that charges the earbuds while they are in your pocket. Pretty cool. However, for some reason, the left earbud either doesn't charge or the charge LED doesn't come on. I have no idea if they will simply stop working or whats going on. At first it would just flicker, and I thought maybe it wasn't sitting right. But no amount of re-settling it in the case will get the light to turn on. It's driving me nuts. Furthermore, after about a day or two, some strange black plastic thing started to appear out of the back of the case, by the hinge. It started to work its way out, and then just kinda came out one day. It was a black square of plastic, about a quarter inch on each side. The case itself doesn't "pop" open when I push the button anymore, and it requires me to press and hold the button and jam a fingernail in there to pull it up. So opening it requires 2 hands and doesn't feel smooth.

All in all, the best thing about these is that there are no wires. The ambient sound feature is pretty cool. I don't use the heart rate monitor at all, and I don't use the ability to save MP3s to the earbuds because I'm always listening to some kind of streaming service. I don't have MP3s anymore. The hassle of them not working right, not charging, not taking my inputs and all the other problems really frustrates me. It's debatable if all the hassle is worth it just to get rid of wires. The thing that might make me switch back to wired headphones is the skipping in my music. At the end of the day, all I want to do is listen to some tunes, and these just screw it up.

I can't believe these cost so much money. They shouldn't be charging more than $35 bucks, MAX.

Anyway, save your money and go buy real headphones. These are trash.

review_text:
Just got my earbuds yesterday.

I immediately charged them, synced them to my Samsung Galaxy Edge 7. Initially, I was impressed by how comfortable they were! The sound was pretty good too... I was impressed by the stereo affect.

After getting set up, I decided to go for a 3 mile run. In the first 1/2 mile, the earbuds kept slipping loose and each time, they would chime a warning saying that connectivity was lost! So I had to continuously re-seat them into my ears and go back to my app (TuneIn Radio) and push play again... This was the case about every 50-100 feat. The good news was that I was so frustrated by having my sound turned off, I didn't pay attention to how tired I was.

Then if that weren't bad enough, before my run was over, the right earbud was completely drained! And the left was nearly dead!

Another drawback was that they didn't seem to work at all unless the GEAR app was open and I had to click "Connect". Would've been nice if they simply auto connected the way other Bluetooth devices do.

Lastly, I decided to try listening to my ear buds while at work today. Again, the comfort was there, but I had to open the Gear app and press connect. They worked well for about 10 mins, but then the seating of the buds in my ear eventually came loose. When they did I near "Disconnected"... I go to re-seat them, but then had to push play in my music app again since it automatically stopped when the Bluetooth lost connection.

I haven't been able to keep them active longer than 10 mins.

Now after I connect them, less than 2 minutes later, same thing... In fact, in the time it took to type this they lost connection at least 10 times!... Wait, it just happened again! (no joke)

After that first 10 minute stretch, they now consistently disconnect about every 30 seconds for no reason.

Going back to wired Bose... but I will switch tips and try again. I want to like these so bad! But right now, they're not worth $50-$80 more than Bose wireless or LG Tones!

I love the concept but they should come with foam earbuds, something that expands in your ear and forms a nice seal and don't slip around. The slightest movement and they slip, which means you'll hear a "Disconnected" message. Maybe it's a software issue... but right now, I'd say wait for their next version.

review_title: Headed for the drawer of tech also means!
review_text:
Having a Galaxy S7 Edge and not a fan of wired headsets, Bluetooth or otherwise I opted to purchase the Gear IconX. This was a major purchasing mistake. I rarely regret my purchase decisions for tech items as I generally perform to the best of my ability, due diligence prior to making the purchase.

In this instance my due diligence failed me. I must admit that I decided to make this purchase the Gear IconX in large part due to my high regard for Samsung products having a Samsung TV, a Galaxy Tablet and my Galaxy S7 Edge. I've had no issues with any of those products. Samsung had become for me a mark of quality.

Everything with this purchase went well. Unfortunately that all ended when it came to actually using the product. I follow a set routine when using a new item. Part of this routine is insuring that any devices involved are fully charged.

In this case both my S7 Edge and the Gear IconX were fully charged with the Gear IconX application installed. Despite all my efforts I'm unable to keep the buds linked to each other or paired to my S7 Edge for more than five minutes at a time. That, of course, makes them totally useless.

The feature set make for an outstanding product and well worth the money if they worked! As it stands, they are consigned to my drawer of tech failures. Fortunately, I also purchased a set of Jabra Sport Elite and they have performed flawlessly.

Samsung would be better served scrapping these IconX and trying again after better R&D.

review_text:
If they worked consistently (or at all, eventually) these would be excellent earbuds. I imagine that the next version or two will be awesome. The fit was really the best I've had and I've always had difficulty fitting earbuds in my weirdo sized ears. These fit snugly and the sound was very good (if a teeny bit quieter than I'd have liked). Certainly loud enough. The ambient sounds feature is cool, but very loud wind when moving at any speed over a leisurely walk makes it more "neat-o" than anything else. Certainly not useful to hear car sounds when running or (definitely not) riding a bike. I never really got a chance to try out the workout bits (i have a watch that does that).

The only thing keeping these from being much higher rated was the difficulty keeping them connected to my Galaxy S7 phone. Audio was jittery and, after about three weeks of use, they now will not connect at all. Nothing. Totally useless as an accessory to my phone. I could store music on them and just use them as standalone music players, but that feature is so limited it's not really suited to how I listen to music. You just load them up and play through the list of songs. No music management beyond that. And the price it pretty steep for a device that doesn't do everything it's designed to do.

I called Samsung to try and troubleshoot, but they S/N printed on the charger didn't come up in their system so my only option is to return them. I'll give these things another shot in a year.

review_text:
After 3 months regular use, the on/off switch stuck. The watch is still somehow usable but major inconvenience.

Edit: I received email from Linking Port (my seller) on 05/06/2021. The email was titled "Thank you for shopping with us. Amazon seller Linking Port has encountered an unexpected problem with completing your order". This title is a little misleading because the order was completed but I was having a product problem. The person by the name of Jessica, representative of customer service from AGPTEK, asked the order number and my address (which she should have already known) and also said she would send me another one. But as you may be experienced this type of thing already, that has never happened (and I have not been expecting). so, please be careful with this company, They try to "pretend" as if they are standing behind customers.

Since my watch is half broken now, I decided to disassemble the watch to see what seems to be wrong. What I noticed is while the perimeter of the watch has a round rubber seal, the on/off switch on the side does not have any seal around it. So, it is reasonably easy to imagine any liquid will enter the inside (especially your sweat that contains salt when you exercise) and stuck around the shaft of the switch. I also found that the tip of the switch inside is designed to push the PCB-like switch to on/off the watch but the PCB-like material is really flimsy and this may break at any time. I do not think the manufacturer performed endurance tests under the reasonably expected conditions like sweating. So, unfortunately my recommendation is not to buy this product. I think most smart watches whose price ranges are around $50, made in China, are the same thing.

review_title: Looks great, not accurate at all
review_text:

Distance measurement isn’t very accurate on the treadmill. It overshoots mileage by about .15 miles per mile versus the treadmill readout. It asks me to calibrate after every workout, so maybe it’s learning and will adjust accordingly. (Edit: Nope.)

The step counter seems to be pretty close.

HR monitor seems undershot. Every other monitor I’ve used, even Garmin’s VivoFit, and the various gym treadmills, pegs me at 170-175bpm full-out. With the VivoActive 3, I’m lucky to break 160. Unless my heart has become substantially stronger suddenly, it seems inaccurate.

The strength app is intuitive and easy for manually recording your reps and sets, but it does a terrible job of sensing an accurate number of reps on its own. If you’re making shorter motions, it barely recognizes that you’re moving. Always underestimates by at least five reps, but usually more.

I haven’t tested it to it’s potential yet, so I may update.

***Update - June 2021***

The heart rate monitor is basically worthless for gym activites. It takes sometimes 20 minutes to finally display anything close to an accurate HR, then it just makes up whatever it wants in that realm. I specifically bought this watch for use as a HR monitor and assumed Garmin would be at least semi-reliable. Not this time.

The only thing this watch does well outside of telling time is look good. Otherwise every smart watch I have ever used outperforms it in basic functionality and accuracy. The battery was advertised by Garmin to last up to 13 days, but my absolute max without bluetooth or any widgets running is three, possibly four.

review_title: Update: Gave me a rash after about 6 months of continued wear & Pace & mileage a little off
review_text:
Update Review 2 Stars December 2018: After about 6 months of continued use, I developed a rash where the heart rate sensor is. I have never had this problem before. The rash took steroid cream and about 2 weeks to go away. Either I became allergic to the metal, or a coating rubbed off the metal and caused irritation. I still wear it just for biking or running, but it is no longer my go to watch. I searched other reviews and many other people have the same problem.

Another thing I realized is that the GPS is not accurate with the speed and mileage. I started noticing this when I ran races and my posted times were always faster than my watch time. Also, this watch shows I come up about .05 to .1 mile short of a measured mile. I have noticed this on 1 mile runs and 10 mile runs, the distance does not matter. I ran with someone with the Fenix 5 Plus and their watch shows an average pace of about 10 to 15 seconds faster per mile than mine does (sometimes 30 seconds). Two stars because I still use it for running and cycling, GPS is quick to locate, pretty accurate HR monitor, links quickly to my Strava account.

Review 5 Stars Feb 2018: I purchased this vivoactive 3 watch in December and I couldn't be happier. I purchased the Fenix 3 last June and returned it. I did not feel it was worth the money. I took it to Kilimanjaro and the elevation data was not accurate at all. In addition, the watch was just to bulky on my wrist. I recently sold my Garmin Edge 1000 bike computer. It had a noisy rattle that I couldn't deal with when riding my bike. It was also a pain to charge and had just too many features that I didn't need. I was looking for something that is simple to use and I could keep track of my runs, rides, and then other miscellaneous workouts all in one place and this is it.

Here is what I love:
It is pretty accurate with my treadmill runs (within a tenth of a mile on a five mile treadmill run)
Accurately tracks my heart rate. I previously had a chest heart rate monitor, and this shows a similar heart rate during my workouts.
I have no issues seeing it during runs or rides in the sun (I live in sunny south Florida)
Holds a decent charge. If I do maybe a 30 minute workout, my battery is at about 85% at the end of the day. I have days where I ride 3-4 hours using the GPS, the battery is at about 60% at the end of that day. I am not sure what it advertises, but for a small watch that does so much, I am happy with the battery life. Charging it every day or every other day isn't a problem for me.
Seamlessly syncs to Strava via the Garmin app on my phone
Quickly picks up GPS
Very comfortable to wear, I am a women with small wrists
Syncs to my phone, so when I am at meetings at work and turn off my phone, this watch buzzes and gives me notifications when I get emails or phone calls
I have been wearing it daily and don't have any scratches to the screen yet (which is pretty amazing because I am hard on my watch)
It has other features that are not as important to me like step counting and stair counting, but they have grown on me as kind of fun metrics to have.

I don't understand the bad reviews. This watch is fantastic for serious triathletes to people beginning a fitness plan (I am somewhere in between), plus it is simple to use. My ultimate watch will be a phone (without carrying my phone on a run), have music (that does not have to be iTunes), and be able to use the Strava live function (when I am out on a run or ride solo, I want someone to know where I am in case something happens). While I am still waiting for my ultimate fitness/phone watch to come out, for $250 this will be good until that materializes.

review_text:
***UPDATE: This thing just gets worse and worse. I'll never buy another Garmin product again. The heartrate monitor is so inaccurate that I don't even look at it. After a big set and I'm gasping for air it reads 80-100 BPM. The battery life if getting worse by the week. Customer service is no help. I REALLY wanted to like this watch. I'll start with what I really hate about it and work backwards to mildly annoying. First off is the automatic face illumination. This idiotic feature wakes up me and my fiancee at least once a night/ morning. It literally lights up the room. Roll over? Go in for a little midnight snuggle? Boom, spotlight in her face, now she's pissed. Brilliant feature from a device that's supposedly tracking my sleep but can't pause this feature while I'm sleeping. Second issue is the button placement. I tried it on the right, I tried it on the left. No matter the orientation, if you bend your wrist you'll inadvertently press the side button and it will start vibrating as it scrolls through the screens with reckless abandon. Third, I feel a lot of the screens are irrelevant to me and I should be able to delete them, or at least rearrange the order... newp. I have to scroll through 8 different things to check my heartrate.... and it goes away after a few seconds so you get to do it again every single time. Brilliant. Fourth, the watch band gets itchy after a few hours. I tried antibacterial soap, talcum powder, nothing works. It stinks after a day or two, also. Lastly, if you don't move for a bit it beeps and vibrates obnoxiously telling you to move. F you, watch....F you. We recently opened a coffee and ice cream shop that's open 15+ hours a day so if we can snag a quick nap we do. It's not for pleasure, strictly survival. Thanks for waking me up mr. piece of junk watch! I SHOULD move, great reminder!
Here's the kick in the nuts. I tried to make this thing work for me, like I said I REALLY wanted to like it. So after a few weeks I decided the relationship was terminal. I contacted Amazon about returning it and they said no dice. We (Amazon and myself) called Garmin. They said I could return it but the refund would take a few months.... so I said forget it. I'll live with this itchy, annoying pos until it dies.

The good: Watch looks great and is stylish. The screen is extremely durable and scratch resistant. The Garmin ecosystem (Connect) is great and intuitive to use. Very much an improvement over the previous Vivoactives

The bad:
- My watch constantly disconnects/reconnects with my android device, and has been for 6 months. Only uninstalling the Connect App and re-connecting the watch fixes it (and temporarily at that). Garmin has not addressed this in any firmware updates
- The other major issue is the fact that I occasionally get battery drains where the watch will burn through a full charge in a matter of hours, despite not participating in any activity. It seems to be tied to the watch auto-updating, or to it trying to secure a bluetooth connection. Only turning the watch off/on a few times corrects this.

Overall I want to like the watch, but given that the power and bluetooth connectivity glitches have not been addressed in some time, I can't recommend this watch to anyone. Will look for another brand for my next watch purchase

Then there is the problem of where the knob lies. It is in just the wrong place. If I happen to move my hand back, angled upwards from the wrist it pushes the knob in EVERY TIME. (Put your hand straight out, then point your fingertips to the ceiling without moving your arm, just angle your wrist and you will understand the motion I am referring to.)

So while the software is fine and the watch LOOKS great, it's product design is not well thought out and, unless I want to have a permanent rash I will have to invest in a different watch.
I have only had this thing for two months now.

I would recommend NOT wasting your money on this particular model of watch.
