review_text:
I wanted to love it but I'm returning it. This device is lightweight, looks great, and fairly comfortable, but the software lets it down. I've had it stop tracking sleep, stop tracking steps and calories until after a full reset, and now, it is counting intensity minutes while I sleep at night. I can rack up 200 minutes a night while sleeping. If I'm really that active, I don't think I need a fitness tracker. At this point, I feel I'm better off without it.

Positives:
- Very lightweight. Coming from Android wear devices, this made me say wow when I first picked it up.
- Good battery. I lost 5-10% per day, which was easily recouped while taking a shower and getting ready in the morning.

Negatives:
- The battery took off on me and use > 20% per day for a couple days, but then I turned location services back on on my phone. I'm not sure if that is related, and if so, why location services on a stationary phone on the counter helps the tracker, but I'm back in the 5-10% range.
- Step and calorie counters stopped recording. Rebooting did not help. I had to manually reset the device to fix it. Its possible this was due to me switching it the day before to record once per second instead of "smartly" and it ran out of recording space. That is just a guess, so who knows...
- I can take the watch off near bedtime and it will report it as "deep sleep" the next day. I don't understand why it doesn't use the HR monitor to help track sleeping. If I'm flatlined, that is beyond a very deep sleep.
- Sleep tracking really only seems useful for seeing how many times I get up at night. Otherwise, it is hit and miss on my memory of when I was wide awake.
- It counts floors, but it wouldn't surprise me if it misses half of them.
- The HR sensor is always recording, but it spikes obscenely at times. I compared the watch against a chest strap and it was within a beat or two while resting, but any activity causes it to overshoot by 10-20 or more bpm. And it appears to do this all day long.

In the end, I have this general feeling that the data I'm looking at isn't so much data as random numbers within a defined range. Yes, I did do about 10 flights of stairs today, but it was probably closer to 14. As I move throughout the day my HR goes all over the place, so whose to say it was 112 or 102 after walking into the kitchen or 92? At this point, I don't trust the data any more than random numbers in the ballpark of what is "normal," and for me at least, that means its going back.

review_text:
First off, I want to say that my expectations were not the highest when my mom got this watch for me on Amazon Prime day. My last smartwatch needed to be charged daily and while this one would not interact with my favorite software, it would still provide almost all the same functionality, with slightly improved styling.

Me being me, I was allergic to the silicone band... It probably had some latex dust on it or something, but wiping the body down with an alcohol wipe and swapping the band out for an easily replaced 22mm band I had on hand was an easy solution. This is something I'm used to and if others are as well, well... Bands are super simple to swap out on this.

Another issue I had with my last smartwatch that I liked about this body was that the recharge pads are recessed. The last watch I had, the contacts corroded and I couldn't charge it and it gave me an infection... This one, the pads are inset quite a ways so that should in no way be an issue. The charger is a clip, however so we'll have to test the longevity of that design. Then again, it won't be used often as you'll see below.

After that, the app was easy to set up and though an update to it wiped my personal data, it doesn't really seem to be much used anyway. The Pedometer seems accurate. The heart rate sensor sometimes takes wild readings if it's too loose, but that's common even to medical readers. The blood pressure calculations seem to be generally accurate - I wouldn't use them for official records, but they're good enough to give you an idea of what your BP is when you're out and about.

The notification setup is lacking and seems to be keyed in mostly for apps I didn't use, but I was able to feel the vibe motor even with the nerve damage in my right arm. The Camera trigger uses the app's built in camera function if you want to stand back and take a selfie - not a bad trick, but more of a gimmick if I'm to be honest, especially since it bypasses your phone's normal app's processing. Still, it can come in handy. The player app, I did not try.

Now for the battery life... I'll admit to being a bit of a battery junky... With the wrist motion turned off as it was just too sensitive and flashed on and off while driving and typing, and with all notifications off and with constant heart rate monitoring on... The battery lasted exactly twenty eight days on the first charge. That's with tapping the single touch point many times a day to check the time and checking my blood pressure and heart rate constantly and with the sleep tracker doing its own thing. Then it charged back up in around an hour. If this keeps up, I've definitely found my new recommendation to people.

Oh and if you're still reading this, here's the bad parts. The screen is not a full touch screen - just the tiny bit at the bottom. Also, the screen seems to only be around 6 bit color or so. It's not the best in color or resolution. Also, when the watch is on, in low light, it's pretty obvious where the edges of the screen are. But hey, for the price and for a month of battery life in such a solid body, I'm not going to knock a star off for that.

While I contemplated purchasing an Apple iWatch, this was her first wearable electronic device, I didn't know how well she'd treat it or if she'd accidently break it. For me... the main seller was the color (pink), the positive reviews on Amazon, and lastly the price.

As I mentioned before...that was a year ago. The watch has held up well and did the intended job. As you can see from the photos or video, it comes with two screen protectors. After traveling to Japan, China, and Iceland with the watch in tow, she is still on the original screen protector. (With proper care) the watch still looks brand new. The battery life is standard in comparison to other smart watches, which is usually a full 24 hours with moderate access/usage.

The watch has several features that make it a "smart watch". It has the time (obviously) with 3-4 backgrounds to choose from (no ability to add more), the ability to connect to wifi, has weather reporting, can play/pause/skip songs on her ipod touch (or android mp3 music player), has a heart rate monitor, has a blood oxygen meter (although I'm unsure how it functions), has a pedometer with daily step tracking and calories burned (several modes), and can receive text messages.

We tether her ipod touch to my iphone and the watch accesses wifi from the ipod touch. Tethering it that way allows her to get text messages to her watch. It definitely makes my daughter happy to get texts on her watch, even if it's just her mother or father telling her to come in and eat dinner. It also allows the watch to pull realtime weather.

Because she has taken such good care of it, we decided to get her an Apple watch this year. This watch was a perfect first "smart watch" at a reasonable price.

review_title: Great value for the price point
review_text:
This is the fifth "smart watch or fitness tracker" device I've bought and the only one I feel that is actually a fair amount of product for the price paid.

Previous purchases either had such garbage battery life I just gave up on them (I already have to charge my phone more than once a day, I sure as hell don't want to have to remember to charge something else) - I'm looking at you Fossil Gen 5) or they were just lacking in the critical features I expect if I'm going to bother dealing with another device.

The Good:
It is a very reasonable price and value. Fifty bucks for a device that reminds me to get up and walk around, tracks steps, has multiple workout types, lets me check the weather, heart rate, time, etc, I can customize the face almost any way I want, the battery lasts for days and days, lets me control music from my wrist, I think is a great value. I was also pleasantly surprised with how useful the Mi Fit app on the phone is. I'm a data nerd and it had enough data to keep me happy.

It does not have onboard GPS, but if you are actually serious enough about specifically being able to track GPS stats for a workout and loathe having your phone in your pocket, you are probably willing to jump to the higher price tier than fifty bucks. The GPS works perfectly when paired to a phone anyway.

The Bad / Weird:

It's basically false advertising to say it has sleep tracking - because it claims it does, but 1. There is literally nowhere on the app or the band to tell it "I'm going to sleep now, start tracking" and 2. It SUPPOSEDLY "automatically tracks when you are sleeping", but it doesn't lol. It thinks I've gotten one and a half hours of sleep every night for the last week. I would literally rate it "utterly useless" for sleep tracking.

When the phone rings, for some bizarre reason the band lets you hang up on someone directly - but if you want to actually pick up the call you have to take your phone out to do so. It's just not a UI design that makes any sense.

In conclusion I think unless you have unreasonably high expectations of it, this is the best value going for this kind of device at this price point.

review_title: Great value and feature rich with mostly good accuracy for all tracking but a small hiccup.
review_text:
The Mi Band 6 is probably one of the best if not the best watches/fitness trackers around this price point. Nice screen, great battery life, and a lot of features, however I as well as some other people have run into heart beat monitoring issues.

What will happen is once you're heavy into exercise, your arm will get sweaty and the Mi Band will start reporting vastly higher heart rates than what is actually going on. For example, during peak cardio my heart will get to mid to high 150s, the Mi Band reported as high as 190, which I know is 100% false, as I have a cheaper Wyze fitness band on at the same time on the other arm, and a treadmill I use at the gym can monitor heart rate as well to confirm more true rates.

The fix is pretty simple, you have to wear the watch even tighter and closer to the wrist (2 to 3 fingers from the wrist) to avoid the sweat messing with the sensors, however that may be some poor design, as a fitness tracker is going to be dealing with sweaty skin, so it shouldn't get tripped up.

Besides that, I've found step, blood oxygen, and sleep accuracy pretty accurate, as I tested with 3 trackers on at the same time (2013 Fitbit Flex, only measures steps and sleep), Wyze Band, and this Mi Band 6.

Modern Fitbits likely have the best sleep accuracy from in depth reviews I've seen on youtube, but I can't justify $100+ for say an Inspire 2 that has a black and white screen with perhaps worse battery life, and fewer features all for some REM cycles being counted better.

You may want to make sure the light is at a high setting before you head out because in sunlight i couldn't read anything or easily increase the light.

The O2 monitor is basically useless. It always shows 95% and I have my rating between 80-92 all the time at the hospital and at home. So don't use it for that!!!

All i all a great price and enough features to keep you going!

review_title: I just wish it was a normal fitness tracker.
review_text:
Update 6/11/2019:

I've had the device about 2 weeks now. It started giving me the wrong time and data, see the image I provided. The app was also wrong too. It's currently ~12:30 and the app was showing it's 11:06AM while the watch itself was jumping between 6 pm, 2 pm, 10 am, etc every few seconds. Not sure what's triggering it and honestly, it's not worth the hassle to fix.

Would not recommend.

----------------------------------------

The fitness tracker portion of it is fine and pretty much exactly what I wanted. The problem is all the extra stuff they added for utility. For example, it comes with a controller for your camera and music on the watch's UI. Well, I don't want to take pictures via the watch, but it shouldn't matter, right? Well, it randomly activates all the fudging time. I'm watching a youtube video while playing with my dog and it randomly switches my video to the camera. I'm listening to music in the gym and brushing against any surfaces with your watch may cause it to pause your music.

Good:
- Battery seems good. I've had it 6 days and it's at 54%. Haven't charged it once yet since the first time but there's a con to the battery too.
- Pretty easy to pair and set it. Basically took 10 minutes or less once it was charged.

Bad:
- The charger seems asinine. I've only charged it once thus far but it took me several attempts before the contacts connected properly. I first opened the packaged and saw that you had to charge it first. I charged it and went out to dinner. Come home to find out that the contacts didn't properly set. Try it again while I play a video game, 45 minutes later, the same thing. The design for charging seems ridiculously finicky compared to others that I have like the Fitbit.
- The button on the watch's face is insanely sensitive. I was walking my dog in a light drizzle of rain and the drops of rain were procing it. I've brushed up against a damp t-shirt and it'll activate the camera. I've just been walking and it'll cycle through the watch's UI. I've noticed it'll proc on a wet t-shirt, my pants, drops of rain, the fur on my dog's back, etc. This wouldn't be that big of a problem if...
- I really, really, really wish there was an option to turn off camera and music player control on the watch. It's driving me insane how often it switches to the camera. I don't take that many pictures as it is and a good 1/10 of my photos are currently random shots taken by the watch while my phone is on a desk or in my pocket. Like Jesus Christ why does it have camera controls?
- Really wish it gave you a battery indicator that's easy to find. I've randomly seen some sort of battery display on the screen as a result of the random UI cycling from how sensitive the face button is, but for the life of me, I haven't found it on purpose yet. The phone app shows what the battery level so it's not that big a deal.

If all this watch thing did was 1) show the time, 2) show your steps per day, 3) show your heart rate, it'll be perfect, but instead, it has this asinine camera and music player controls that is the most annoying thing I've ever had.

review_title: It does some things well, at least
review_text: I purchased this as an affordable way to track my heart rate, stress, and blood oxygenation throughout the day. It does all of those things fairly reliably and accurately, although it would be nice if it checked blood oxygenation automatically. Currently, this needs to be initiated manually. It also appears to track sleep fairly accurately, although, again, it would be nice if the sleep tracking included continuous blood oxygen readings. The app currently provides a metric related to breathing quality during sleep, but it's unclear how this metric is derived, since it doesn't appear to use any SpO2 readings. The mobile app situation is confusing. There are two apps that appear to work for this device. The app recommended in the manual, Mi Fitness, has a somewhat nicer user interface, but lacks Google Fit integration. The other app (which appears more popular), Zepp Life, doesn't look as nice, but has Google Fit integration and allows you to use Imperial measurements. It's unclear whether there's any feature loss from using Zepp Life, which appears to be made by a subsidiary of Xiaomi that produces the slightly less expensive AmazFit line of smart fitness products. My major qualm with the Mi Band 6 is that it doesn't count steps well. This is the most basic of features. Pedometers have been doing this well since before smartphone connectivity was a thing. But the Mi Band 6 only registers steps if I emphatically swing my arms when I walk. Compared to my phone, an old Fitbit, and a Pebble watch, it undercounts steps by around 65%. It also falsely registers steps when I raise my arm to look at my phone, or lower my arm to my lap after typing on my keyboard. I feel like I mostly got what I paid for, but lack of step-countimg functionality is pretty ridiculous. If I were to buy again, I'd probably go for the less expensy AmazFit, which seems to have all the same functionality, the same app, plus Alexa integration, but has fewer activities / workout types.

review_title: Apple has screwed up the charging
review_text:
I have given this a lower rating of 2 because of Apple's stupidity. The watch itself is fine and should be rated higher. However, on the 7-series and on the latest iPad's, Apple has changed the charging cord on both ends. Both the insert connector to the power source and the connector to the watch (iPad) are different from previous versions and are not compatible with previous chargers. The power source can no longer be a USB port as the connector doesn't fit. And old charging cords cannot be used as they don't fit the iWatch or the iPad. This means you have to have double sets of chargers around, including automobile charges It is very annoying and irritating. Why did Apple do this?

In addition, I unplug the charger from my iPad at my own peril. When I reconnect it it doesn't always start charging. I have to fiddle with the connections on both ends, and even the AC adapter until it starts charging. This makes me leery about removing the charger to take the iPad elsewhere. It is not the cords or AC adapter as two sets do the same thing.

Is it just me or do others feel that Apple has gone downhill since Steve Jobs is not longer there.

I am a middle distance runner and run at least 30 mins/day, 6 days/week.  Apple watch gives varying distances most of the time I run on a course, even though I run the same course each time.  Speeds are not accurate and will fluctuate 1+ minute per mile whenever i run on a track, depending on which direction I run on the track.  The heart rate tracker is extremely inaccurate and is the most inaccurate part.  There are times that I will go on a 30 min run without getting a single accurate heart rate.  Other times, it will register a 210 bpm heart rate AS SOON AS I BEGIN RUNNING, and will stay extremely high for 10-15 mins before dropping down to my normal heart rate.  Apple watch works great for other smart watch functions, but is hands down the worst fitness tracker.  DO NOT BUY IF YOU ARE ONLY LOOKING FOR A GOOD FITNESS TRACKER.  SAVE YOUR MONEY AND LOOK ELSEWHERE.

review_title: I was hoping it would not happen to me...
review_text:
I have been a Fitbit customer since Fitbit Charge came out. This year I kept making sure I waited until the next set of Fitbit Smart Watches came out before I purchased the Sense 2. The Sense 2 and Versa 4 had bad ratings, but I kept waiting until I can read more reviews. Each review that came out stated that the new versions were not great since they don't support 3rd Party apps, Gmail and Calendar so it’s better to purchase the previous versions. I also checked the features and On-wrist calls, Google Maps, and Google Wallet are supposed to be implemented but they don’t have a specific date either, so it was making me consider the previous versions more.

I was also hesitant to buy the Fitbit Sense since my family member told me she had gotten burned with her Fitbit and I saw others did not have those issues in the reviews, so I decided to give it a try anyways. I finally bought the Sense and was excited and took the time to set it up. The clock faces were nice the interface was so easy to use, and it felt like I had gotten reunited with an old friend. I wore the watch for 13 hrs. I woke up the next morning getting ready for work and my wrist was feeling uncomfortable, so I took my watch off and a perfect red shape of the back of the watch was there and it was itching. I waited a bit and the rash/burn started getting smaller.

- Do I need to keep taking it off after a few hours?
- Can I use it for sleep tracking?
- What about my steps… will the count be consistent if I can’t wear my watch while I am active?

I need to be able to wear the watch and that was the reason why I bought it.

Sad to say… Loyal Long Time Fitbit User has left the building… Apple Watch or Garmin here I come!

review_text:
I've been using it for 7 months and all I can say is that I'm disappointed.

These is the list of issues so far:
- The app keeps disconnecting from the Sense, I need to manually pull up my phone and get it re-synced all the time.
- No sleep score while the Sense is disconnected from the app (which is most of the time).
- Awful WiFi performance.
- Poor selection of clocks, in fact, I use only the default one. Also, some clocks are geo-blocked.
- Poor selection of apps in general.
- Timer only supports up to 99 minutes. Very poor! I have a Casio from the 90's which supports setting up timers for days, even weeks. This was particularly annoying, because I had a task that needed to be repeated every 24 hours with precision, and I couldn't set up a 24-hour timer.
- No smart brightness control, so it burns my eyes when I look at it at night.
- Heart rate sensor is inaccurate.
- Oxygen meter sensor is inaccurate and slow.
- Battery life is subpar.
- The arm gesture to turn the screen on only works 50% of the times (sometimes I look like an idiot raising my arm three of four times, because it simply won't turn on sometimes).
- Pro features behind an expensive paywall.
- GPS only works when an exercise program is on instead of all the time. I thought I was going to be able to pull up some nice map indicating where I've been during the day, and it's not the case.
- Sometimes it's slow.
- It's waaaay less cool than the Apple watch, and being that this is 300 USD, if you can shell out the extra 99 USD that the Apple watch costs you are getting a way better value for the money.
- Google is making this product obsolete in the short term when they release their newest watch.

Most who have purchased Fitbit devices know how this works: "Your device is out of warranty, but here's a 25% coupon off of a new one." Well, that brings the price down to what Amazon charges and I get free 2-day shipping.

I am an Android/Google user...But all I can think when I have trouble with this truly terrible product is "This would never, ever happen with an Apple watch."

The battery life is great. The band is cheap and awful.

review_title: Product Life Span Not Worth The Price
review_text:

I called customer service and they walked me through a factory reset and it started working again (YAY!) Last friday, it stopped charging. I tried every type of outlet I could think of, did the instructed cleaning as suggested on the site, called customer service which recommended the same actions and no luck. A year and two months later, a $300 watch is dead. I am now out of warranty but Fibit did offer me a 35% off on a new watch to be used within the next 30 days. I am torn, because I have used fitbits for years and the more expensive the watch is, the shorter the life span.

As for the product itself, when it was working, I did love it. It mapped my runs, had so many exercise options, and had relaxing tools. I love the app. You can track your food on it, connect with friends (I have weekly step count competitions with my mom and sister for fun). The biggest disapointment was the lifespan. I will not be purchasing the sense again as there were too many issues. I also find it interesting that when you call customer service, they have a selection dedicated to the Sense product specifically. I really wish this had been a more reliable product with longevity.

Battery life is consistently less than 48 hours. I must now recharge it daily or it dies during the second night. Because of this, it can't reliably be used as an alarm. I would gladly go back to my 3 year old Versa 1 if I hadn't given it to my son.

=== Original ===
I finally traded my original Versa in for a Sense about a month ago. So far, I really like the Sense for the most part, but there are a few problems for me.

Pros:
Screen is beautiful.
Fit and finish are superb. It feels really nice and the band feels plenty secure.
Additional sensors are nice. Some complain about accuracy, but I have nothing to compare them to.

Cons:
The subscription service is just insulting.
The "button" is weirdly difficult to actuate. I have to position my hand just right to get it to work.
Battery life is atrocious. My 3 year old Versa could generally go close to a week on a charge. This new Sense sometimes barely lasts 2 days. And it seems to correlate to my activity level. I hope they can fix the software to improve battery life.

review_title: Originally seemed great–stopped working after 3 months!
review_text:
I bought this after 2.5 years of using Fitbit HR (1st & 2nd gen), and in that time had 6 warranty replacements due to hardware defects. The final Fitbit died a week out of warranty at which point I have given up on using Fitbit products again. As for the Mi Band 4 that I bought to replace it:

The Good:
•Battery life is amazing after coming from Fitbit. I had continuous HR and all notifications on and I could still go 2-3 weeks on a 2 hour charge.
•The color screen is so much nicer than the Fitbit bands I previously used.
•The overall build quality seems pretty good. It can be a bit awkward to take the unit out of the band and replace after charging, but I do like that the bands can be replaced cheaply in many styles and colors.
•The app is not as intuitive as Fitbit, but it is perfectly useable.
•Being waterproof for swimming and showering is nice, although when showering the water often registers as a touch on the screen.
•The price, for what you are getting is a pretty good deal.
•When it is set to always on, the heart rate tracking seems pretty accurate. I have over 2 years of tracking data from Fitbit, which seams to correspond almost identically to my 3 months data from the Mi Band.

The Bad:
•If you are buying it for sleep tracking, don't bother, the accuracy is terrible. That said, the Fitbit devices I had were equally bad.
•The step counter is very accurate when you are walking regularly, however, it fails to register any steps if you have the hand resting on a bar while moving, such as on a lawn mower, treadmill desk, stroller or shopping cart. The calibration on my Fitbit seemed to deal with this OK, but the Mi Band will be lucky to register even a single step.
•Notifications seem to be hit and miss. I seem to get every tidal alert several times a day, but call and message notifications only a small percentage of the time.
•The single biggest problem and the reason for the one star review, is that after 3 months the touch screen no longer responds. I have tried running the battery flat and recharging, and after following forum advice to unpair the device, it will no longer pair as you need to accept the pairing by touching the screen on the band! I feel like you are getting great tech for $36, but I expect more than 3 months for the money. If it had lasted a year or more, I would probably just buy another one, but as it is I can't recommend it and will be looking for another alternative.

review_text:
I have been using this band for about a month now and here are my observations:

The good:

-It is sleek and comfortable.
-It is water resistant. Didn't get damaged at all during showers and swimming.
-Battery life is great. You don't need to charge it more often than once every other week.
-Its step counter appears accurate.

The Meh:

-The app is a bit counter-intuitive and don't offer much in terms of integrating with other apps on your phone: just whatsapp and google fit. I wish it connected with gmail.
-Water activates the screen randomly. If you are in the pool and want to check your heartrate or see a message, good luck.

The Bad:
-This device is wildly inaccurate in measuring heart rate, calories burnt and sleep. It has at least a 30% error margin in heart rate measurement. I checked by counting my pulse with a stopwatch. It can read anywhere between 70 to 130 when you have a pulse of 100. The app underestimates caloric expenditure by 30-50%, when you compare it to the estimates by other apps like googlefit and myfitnesspal, and any caloric calculator you find on the net. This is bizzare because you enter your weight and height when you register the app. I am not sure about how bad it is in measuring your sleep, but I know that when I lie in the bed for 20 minutes in the morning and chitchat with my wife, it still thinks I am asleep. For all I know, I could be waking up 10 times every night from sleep apnea and this band wouldn't notice any of them.

Verdict: If you want a step-counting watch that alerts you to phonecalls and whatsapp messages by vibrating, this is good. If you intend to use it for monitoring your heart rate, dietary needs or sleep, it is useless.

After years of using Pebble and Amazfit watches I decided to go Apple Watch because of the heart monitoring features and solid support for my iOS devices (phone, tablet). The watch works great. Getting it setup with my iPhone 12 Pro was just a non-event. It worked instantly.

The display is amazing. Just gorgeous. The reaction time with using the screen, crown, or button is instant. No lag at all.

The only issue I have is the battery. I never went to Apple Watch before Series 7 because 24 or less hours of battery life and having to carry a custom charging base everywhere I got is just untenable.

Series 7 docs state even with always on display the average is a goal of 18 hours. HA. I'm lucky to get 10 or 12 and it doesn't even do much during the day. I've tested others like several Android watches over the years too and none were this consumptive of battery.

The sleep tracking works fine, but it's not comfortable to wear in bed all night. I don't think any "band" is.

Overall, I like it. I'll use it. It works super well with my iPhone and the apps are great. But honestly, if I had known the battery life was this short with average usage, I would have probably gone with another Amazfit or the Pebble based FitBit Versa 3.

review_title: Android Fanboy Finally Gets An Apple Watch
review_text:
Okay, I've been an Android fan since, well, since the very beginning...I still am if I'm being honest. I have also spent a ridiculously large amount of $$ on smart watches over the years starting with the original Moto 360 (anyone remember that flat tire?). It LOOKED cool, especially that round face, but performance-wise, well, it was kinda terrible. The battery life was insultingly horrible (it would lose 7% in the ten minute drive to work while just sitting on my wrist doing nothing). But the potential was there. In finally switched to Samsung's Tizen at the introduction of the Gear S2. What a great watch that was. I went on to the Gear S3, the Gear Sport, the Galaxy Watch, the GW3 and then I heard the news: Samsung was going back to Wear OS. This disappointed me greatly. Over the years I have owned well over a dozen watches utilizing Wear OS (or Android Wear before that) and while I loved a lot about many of them, they ALL suffered from the stuttering and glitching that plagues essentially ALL Wear OS devices. Some have managed to work around that to produce the best version they possibly can (TicWatch Pro 3 and the Oppo Watch are just 2 examples) but each had at least something that just didn't work properly - and I don't blame either manufacturer for this. It's an ongoing problem with Wear OS itself. Slowly, I began to warm to the idea that maybe, just MAYBE Samsung will make it work the way it was always supposed to work. So, I bought the Galaxy Watch 4.

Did Samsung fix Wear OS? In a word: NO. It still suffers from glitches, hiccups and stuttering and apps not opening properly and/or timely. At times it works just great (which is more often than not, but still...), I have a fairly expensive watch that ruins what otherwise ought to be a smoother experience than what I'm getting. My Galaxy Watch 3 runs fantastic (it runs on TIzen software and not Wear OS) and honestly, I have had zero issues with it since I got it over a year ago, nor any with my previous Tizen watches including the Gear S2, S3, Gear Sport and original Galaxy Watch. I have had intermittent issues with the GW4 since the day I brought it home. To be fair, I have heard many people who claim that their Watch 4's have run flawlessly since they bought theirs...but I cannot speak to their experience, only the one I've had - but I brought it up to be fair.

I have done a LOT of research regarding all different kinds of smart watches, and you know what you almost never hear from the majority of apple watch owners? You don't hear about not getting a notification, or stuttering and glitches here and there. Sure, I'm sure they exist, but the overwhelming majority generally say the same thing: the watch JUST WORKS. Honestly, that is all I really care about. Does it do what it claims and does it do it consistently? From an Android Fanboy, I can say this without reservation: the apple watch works and does so CONSISTENTLY. I simply cannot say that about my GW4 or any other Wear OS device I have used over the last 6-8 years.

Okay, now why did I switch? Well, when I heard that the apple watch could be used without an iPhone, it really caught my attention. Seriously, an apple watch that can be set up so the user does not need an iPhone?? Well that's just what I wanted to hear. The truth is, once the watch is set up with "Family Setup" as long as it's an LTE model watch, you do not need to have it paired with an iPhone AT ALL...however (and this is a biggie) - you STILL need an iPhone to set it up initially. That sucked. But - I have enough friends with iPhone's that I took the plunge anyway.

The watch looks phenomenal BTW. I got the blue model and that new watch face that takes advantage of the larger screen is fantastic. Since this is my very first apple watch, I can't speak to how well it compares to earlier models, so I'm sorry about that. Honestly however, having not used a previous model before, I just don't see that there is a difference that is noticeable when compared to my friends who have earlier model apple watches. The major thing I like is exactly what I wanted most: a watch that is reliable. It took a bit of getting used to because I have been so familiar with Wear OS and Tizen watches for so long, but it isn't difficult, just takes a little time, that's all. I haven't always liked the apple rectangular shape...but slowly, it grew on me. It was always made really well, of that there has never been any doubt, but the series 7 is just great to look at.

The one thing keeping my review from 5 to only 4 stars was the pretty HUGE omission of the charging block. As you've no doubt gathered by now, I'm a android guy and always have been. My last 4 phones have all used USB-C chargers...but none of them came with blocks that the USB-C cord went into, they all had the USB-C port on only ONE end, not both. It's fair to assume the majority of apple users do not own one of these, either. Meaning, it's an unnecessary EXTRA expense you absolutely MUST make in order to even be able to use your watch - unless you have a charger from a previous apple watch which you can still use, but you won't be able to take advantage of the faster charging time. For what apple is charging for this watch, leaving this out is nothing shy of a ginormous cash grab on their part, and it's rather blatant and disappointing. Seriously guys, this is simple greed...and if anyone at their HQ bothers to read any of these reviews will note that there are quite a few upset genuine apple fanatics who really are quite upset by this same situation, so I am definitely NOT alone here. Wise up apple or you'll force longtime fans into the arms of Wear OS simply to make a statement.

With that said, the watch operates extraordinarily well. I have seen zero hiccups that I see each time I turned on my Galaxy Watch 4 (seriously, EVERY time I turn it on, I get a notification that tells me I have voice mail, but when I check, there is nothing there - literally EVERY SINGLE TIME I turn the watch on. After 3 months...it got old...and now it simply makes me mad). I've always heard of the great haptics on apple devices and now I know what they mean. Samsung does a pretty good job as well on their watches, don't get me wrong, but these are just, well, better. It's hard to describe unless you've actually worn one to feel the difference. My TicWatch Pro 3 is actually a pretty good Wear OS watch, it really is...however, the haptics are so friggin' anemic I miss 90% of my notification vibrations due to the poor haptic engine it has. (this is an issue with hundreds of thousands of other TicWatch Pro 3 owners...it's on many online threads if you're curious) That isn't the case here with the series 7. I get ALL my notifications and in a timely manner and that on-screen keyboard with swipe-like ability is fantastic. It's not as good as the Google keyboard, but it isn't far behind...and for quick text input, especially if you're in a loud environment where you cannot use voice dictation, or you're in a quiet place or you simply don't want people around you to hear what you're replying, this is a wonderful tool and it works pretty great. Kudos to apple for adding it. I want to mention the haptic engine again...it's actually quite impressive. It vibrates in a totally different manner than ALL other smart watches I've ever owned. It works beautifully and it is hard to miss a notification due to it's efficiency. I swear, if my TicWatch had a decent haptic engine and better music-transfer capability, I may never have even considered getting the apple watch at all.

This the only smartwatch besides Samsung to make transferring music to your watch pretty seamless. OR SO I THOUGHT. I tried almost a dozen different programs supposedly designed to help convert my mp3's to easily transfer to my phone and then onto my watch. Almost every one would cap you at transferring 10 songs per day ONLY - unless you paid money. Even iTunes was a problem saying that I had to change this setting on my phone in order to transfer music...yet no matter how often I changed the setting, it still said I needed to do the same thing again. I deleted iTunes and re-downloaded it and tried again. Nope. Same issue. I finally discovered a program called, "SynciOS" which allowed me to transfer music in a pretty intuitive manner and do it ridiculously quick. Not sure why it took so long to be able to do something so simple, but sheesh, this was essentially the only thing that really frustrated me regarding my series 7 watch. Samsung makes this process STUPID EASY to do and sorry apple fans, is FAR SUPERIOR to how apple does it. All other Wear OS watches are no better at making this an easy process and in fact, can make it even more difficult.

I love how on my hikes, while listening to music on my watch, I'll get updates every mile I've reached. This is another great feature...but its one that is done better with the Galaxy Watches. The Original GW and the GW3 and GW4 all give you this same information but goes a few steps further. Samsung tells you when you've reached that mile, but also tells you how many steps you've taken to get there AND your heart rate. It only takes 3-4 extra seconds and it works great. The difference between Tizen and Wear OS however is that with TIzen the music would halt while the watch reads out that info thru the bluetooth earbuds, while Wear OS it just slightly lowers the volume of music and tells you the information. Apple lowers the music volume much lower which makes hearing your metrics much easier, but still, the more information the better as far as I'm concerned. Yesterday I wore both my GW3 and the apple watch and they each marked every mile within probably 4-5 seconds of one another - or roughly 15-20 feet difference, which says they both were pretty spot-on for how they measured distance. They both were within about 7 steps of each other as well and heart rate were off by 1 or 2 beats per minute. That tells me either they are both accurate, or both are off by roughly the same amount. There may be a few workout routines that apple doesn't cover which Samsung does and vice versa, but they do all the one's I personally use regularly and that's what counts as far as I'm concerned. Great implementation, too.

All in all, you've made this Android user a convert. Though, I still prefer using my Samsung phone. Sorry guys.

***UPDATE***

Battery life compared to my GW4 is simply astonishing - especially considering how much people whine about it online. Case in point: yesterday I braved the snow and 15 degree temps and walked the 5 miles home from work for my exercise. I wore both my Galaxy Watch 4 and apple watch 7. Keep in mind before I left, I topped off my GW4 til it was at 100%, something I could not do with my apple watch since I do not have a spare charger at work like I do with my Samsung watches, which seem to need it more often. I will stipulate that after a few weeks using my GW4 the battery life improved significantly as it "learned" my habits and adjusted accordingly. I used GPS on both to keep track of my walk, and listened to music downloaded to both watches and switched from one to the other exactly at the half-way point to make it fair. By the time I reached home, my GW4 was down to 61%. Now keep in mind I had been using my apple watch since 5am that morning and wasn't able to charge it before leaving for home. When I hit home my apple watch 7 was still at 79%. That is astonishing to me...and an enormously HUGE difference. I have suspected the battery life was better, but not by THAT much. I just looked it up, and the 45mm apple Watch 7 has a battery size of 309 mAh, while the GW4 has a battery size of 361 mAh. Sorry, but this is a GINORMOUS apple win here. It seems every other review I read about the newest apple watch, one of the chief complaints is battery life, but when compared to the GW4, I cannot help but be happy with it's performance so far. After having used the apple watch for over a week, using the GW4 reminded me (again) that Wear OS just isn't quite there yet. The crazy glitches that plague this system, the incessant notification of voicemail that is NEVER there 100% of the time whenever I turn the watch off and turn it back on again, the notification that my watch is playing media that isn't there, or that it's paired with a kindle that I have never paired it with, the slowness of opening apps and closing them again, the problem of pulling down the settings menu and how it works about half the time I try to pull it down, or scroll up working only part of the time, or how I close all apps only to discover some still open - apps I've never tried to open since the day I bought my watch...the list goes on and on. You know what glitches I've had with the apple watch? NONE. Seriously. I haven't had one single hiccup since I turned this device on. I truly wished this were not the case with my Samsung. The honest truth is I wouldn't even have an apple watch were it not for my sour experience with the newest Galaxy Watch. I still hope that a future update will correct most of these problems, and if so, I will be thrilled to see them implemented and will gladly state so. Problem is, I don't think this is Samsung's problem, it's an issue with Wear OS and Samsung can only do so much to correct it. I DO find it interesting that my older TicWatch Pro 3 has shown far fewer issues and glitches than the GW4 in pretty much every situation...so maybe its a combination of Wear OS and Samsung's version of Wear OS 3.0. Either way, I've been very disappointed in my experience and wish that they had never switched from Tizen in the first place. Oh well. Time will tell if Wear OS can correct these issues or not.

The body composition feature is cool on the GW4. I really thought it would be more useful, though. I suppose it can be, but - for me at least - it simply hasn't been something that I've been able to get any kind of genuine use out of. Reportedly it can actually measure your blood pressure...but on a watch? I honestly cannot see how accurate that could be using any kind of method the way the watch is set up. Every reputable medical site I have looked at says the tech is far too new and simply isn't capable - yet anyway - of accurately being able to measure blood pressure monitoring. Kudos to Samsung for initiating it, but at this point, I wouldn't put a whole lot of stock on accuracy.

Charging...so, since this is my first apple watch, I can't compare it's supposedly 33% faster charging over previous models...but I WILL say it's faster than the Galaxy Watch 4, 3, Original Galaxy Watch etc. and my TicWatch Pro 3...however, I have an Oppo Watch (which was clearly a ripoff of the apple watch design, but in their defense, they did a STELLAR job with it), now that watch charges FAST. Exactly how much faster, I cannot say for certain, but let's just say all of those other models I mentioned pale in comparison. I just find it absurd that apple did not include a charging block. An utterly imbecilic decision.

review_title: Great if you have a Samsung phone
review_text:
Pros:
+ Light
+ Battery better than expected (details later)
+ Convenient
+ Good use of screen
+ ECG and body composition measurements with Samsung phone
+ Half brightness is still pretty bright

Cons:
- Fitness tracking can be iffy
- Some features require a Samsung phone
- Not sure about ECG but the body composition feature isn't really accurate. It's a watch so it's not meant to be super accurate.

Battery life:
I have always on display turned off, brightness set to about quarter to half brightness, heart rate monitor measuring continuously, NOT on airplane mode. I also have it set up such that when raise my wrist to look at my watch, the screen turns on. The battery lasts far longer than a day for me. I'm not sure what those other reviewers are doing to kill the battery so quickly. My guess is they have the brightness at 100% and always on display turned on as well as a bunch of other features/apps running in the background. Of course that would kill the battery...

Fitness tracking:
The watch always detects workouts late as well as when they stop. I would say it takes a minute before it "realizes" I have stopped doing some activity. Another thing is that the app kind of sucks when it comes to this. I lift more than anything and a good majority of the stuff I do isn't listed. Furthermore, I just want to know how long I have been active, my heart rate, and an estimate of the calories I have burned. The app makes it a bit annoying to do this. I definitely liked the simplicity of the FitBit app more. Also, the heart rate monitor can be finicky when I'm sweating heavily. Sometimes it just can't detect my heart rate. I guess that's just a limitation of smart watches in general though (if you want an accurate and precise hr monitor, get a chest strap).

Body composition:
It's decent for what it is. Measurements are never accurate (it says my body fat percentage is 30+ but I know I'm closer to the 20-25 range). It measures BMI, water weight, muscle weight, and a few other details too. review_text:
This watch has been a pleasure to use. Both the software and hardware have been upgraded, and the price has gone down compared to previous models. As an avid Android user (Galaxy S21), the integration with my phone is very tight. I'd only recommended this watch if you are a Samsung user, however.

Samsung's spin on Wear OS is a welcome change, though those coming from Tizen won't notice many differences on the front end. Google services like Maps and Messages are epic, not to mention all the other apps in Play Store (which is objectively superior to Samsung's Galaxy Store, though that still exists and cannot be deleted).

Sleep tracking is great, though I wouldn't trust it religiously. Same goes with the Bioactive sensors that measure body fat percentage and water mass. These are awesome features but have been somewhat inconsistent in my unscientific experiments. Luckily, these things can improve over time with software updates. My pervious Samsung watch had troubling measurements at launch but consistently improved in the months following, so I'm not worried.

The design is now boxier and more modernized, though I've found that this actually makes using the touch bezel harder to use because the edges of the watch don't slope as much as before. The watch you see in the photo is the 40mm version with the silver sport band.

Battery life is probably the biggest con of this watch. Samsung promises 40 hours, which I've found to be a pathetic overestimate considering my "normal" usage rate. You can turn off the Always On Display and workout detection to squeeze a few extra hours, but don't expect it to last longer than 2 days.

Overall I'm very pleased with this watch and would recommend it to any Samsung user. Other non-Samsung users (and non-iOS users) will miss out on a couple of features like the ECG and Bioactive measurements, but can still use almost every other basic feature.

review_text: the mi fit band is a great beginner band for someone who wants to start tracking distance and heart rate while running outside. It has GPS which is a feature that most of the lower end bands do not have. The heart rate is fairly accurate. I wouldn't really use this for sleep tracking because it can't tell youre awake unless you physically get up. The band itself is comfortable but can be awkward to clasp closed. Battery life is amazing.

review_text: I had heard good things about the mi band 3 and was considering buying one so when the mi band 4 came out for $40 I decided to go ahead. I could never justify spending $150+ on a fitness tracker or smart watch. This watch alerts you to incoming calls, notifications, etc and the battery is probably its shining attribute. Setup was a little quirky with all the instructions in Chinese. If you have trouble pairing to the app, place the mi band on the charger then try again. That's what worked for me. I love the step tracker and multiple display themes. Way better deal than a fitbit
